title: Dilbert Tells Date He's a Witch

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't believe she agreed to have dinner with me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid to say anything to spoil this moment...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I guess I should say something to break the ice.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Did I mention that I'm a witch?

setting: A restaurant, as Dilbert and his dinner date arrive at their table
situation: Dilbert walks into a restaurant with a woman who has agreed to have dinner with him. He thinks happily about his luck, then worries about saying anything that might ruin the moment. When he decides to break the ice, the woman is the one who speaks, announcing that she is a witch.
punchline: Dilbert's date beats him to the conversation and drops an alarming, awkward confession that is the opposite of safe small talk.
summary: A nervous man planning how to start conversation on a rare dinner date is upstaged when his companion casually reveals she practices witchcraft.

title: Library Reference Desk Knows Everything

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hello, is this the library reference desk?

transcript.speaker: Reference Librarian (phone)
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the average running speed of the Tazmanian Boola-Boola dog?

transcript.speaker: Reference Librarian (phone)
transcript.text: 8.3 miles per hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't believe she knew that.

transcript.speaker: Reference Librarian (phone)
transcript.text: And you have something stuck in your teeth.

setting: Dilbert's location, on the phone with a library
situation: Dilbert phones the library reference desk and asks for the running speed of an obscure, invented animal. The librarian answers instantly and precisely. Dilbert marvels at her knowledge, and she then adds that he has something stuck in his teeth, implying she can see him.
punchline: The librarian's omniscience extends beyond trivia to watching Dilbert himself, revealing she can see him through the phone.
summary: A man tests a librarian with an absurd animal question, only to discover her knowledge reaches right into his own mouth.

title: Hypnotized Into Buying Worthless Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Hypnotist
transcript.text: ...After you leave you will not remember being inside your computer talking to a micro-chip.

transcript.speaker: Hypnotist
transcript.text: You will purchase worthless computer upgrades and argue that it saves money in the long run.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a static byte dwinkelizer... a necessity really.

setting: Hypnotist's office with a swinging pendant, then Dilbert's chair with a keypad device
situation: A hypnotist in a red hooded costume swings a pendant in front of Dilbert and gives him post-hypnotic suggestions. He plants the idea that Dilbert will forget a vivid experience inside his computer and will instead buy pointless computer upgrades while claiming they save money. In the last panel Dilbert sits with a gadget in hand, parroting the suggestion and defending a made-up component as a necessity.
punchline: The hypnotist's commands are really a description of how people already behave as technology consumers: buying useless upgrades and rationalizing them with jargon and false savings claims.
summary: Under a hypnotist's spell, Dilbert is programmed to waste money on useless gear and to insist with technobabble that it was a sensible investment.

title: Digging a Hole for Dirt

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I'll make a room for the baby by digging a cavern under Dilbert's closet.

transcript.speaker: Dawn
transcript.text: Where will you put all the dirt?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Obviously I'll have to dig a second hole to hold all the dirt.

setting: Inside the dinosaur couple's home, next to a closet door in Dilbert's house
situation: Bob the green dinosaur announces he will make a nursery for the baby by digging a cavern under Dilbert's closet. His mate Dawn asks where he will put all the dirt. Bob confidently replies that he will simply dig a second hole to hold it.
punchline: Bob's solution to the dirt problem is circular, since a second hole would create yet more dirt that needs somewhere to go.
summary: A dinosaur planning an underground nursery solves his excavation problem with a hole-digging plan that creates the very problem it is meant to fix.

title: Mother Nature Evicts Humanity

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Okay, everybody off! Let's go, get off!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mother Nature?

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Move along now. Find another planet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But... But...

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Shoo! Come back when all the plastic is gone.

setting: Outdoors against a blue sky background, on Earth
situation: A sunglasses-wearing Mother Nature, waving a stick like a bouncer or shepherd, orders everyone off the planet. A confused Dilbert asks if she is Mother Nature and protests as she tells humanity to find another planet. She shoos him away and says they can return once the plastic is gone.
punchline: Mother Nature evicts humans from Earth, implying that plastic pollution is so persistent that humanity won't be welcome back for a very long time, if ever.
summary: The personification of nature kicks humans off the planet and tells them to leave until all their long-lasting plastic waste has disappeared.

title: Eyes Follow You Home

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: Notice how the eyes seem to follow you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow, that's a weird effect.

transcript.speaker: Curator
transcript.text: It gets better.

setting: An art gallery, then Dilbert's home
situation: A gallery curator points out to Dilbert that the eyes in a painting seem to follow the viewer, and Dilbert calls it a weird effect. The curator hints that it gets better. In the last panel Dilbert is at home reading a newspaper in his chair while a pair of eyes peers in at him from the dark window.
punchline: The curator's promise that the effect gets better turns out to mean the eyes literally follow Dilbert home, as a stalker watches him through his window.
summary: A museum guide's creepy art tip becomes literal when a pair of watching eyes turns up outside Dilbert's living room window.

title: Dilbert Pleads With Mother Nature

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Please, Mother Nature, don't make me leave the Earth!!

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Don't talk back to me!!

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: I work hard to give you a lovely planet, and look what you do to it!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But... but I recycle newspapers!

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Oh, well, excuse me. I guess the dolphins are safe, thanks to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And I've noticed less acid rain since I started.

setting: A blank blue background, standing in for the Earth itself
situation: Dilbert begs Mother Nature, a sunglasses-wearing woman wielding a switch, not to make him leave the planet. She whips him and scolds him for what humanity has done to the Earth. Dilbert defensively points to his newspaper recycling, and she sarcastically mocks his claims.
punchline: Dilbert's pitiful recycling effort is absurdly small next to humanity's environmental damage, and he foolishly takes credit for saving dolphins and reducing acid rain.
summary: A man tries to excuse his tiny green habit to a furious, whip-wielding personification of nature who is unimpressed by his claimed achievements.

title: Rejected Date, Social Security Number Excuse

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sorry, I don't date guys from work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll resign...

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sorry, I don't date unemployed guys.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I... I'll get a new job... one you approve of.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Sorry, I don't date guys with your Social Security number.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, it turns out her unlucky number has nine digits in it...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But she knew my Social Security number, so I think there's some interest there...

setting: Office, then Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert asks a female coworker out and keeps offering to change his circumstances as she shoots down each excuse, first quitting his job and then getting a new one. Her final rejection absurdly targets his Social Security number. Afterward, Dogbert points out the number's flaw while Dilbert clings to the belief that she must be interested because she knew it.
punchline: Dilbert interprets a flat rejection as a sign of interest because she knew his Social Security number, ignoring that her excuse was absurd and that she is clearly just making up reasons.
summary: A hopeful man keeps getting turned down with ever sillier reasons yet convinces himself there is still a spark.

title: Dogbert Becomes a Substitute Teacher

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You what?!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I got a job as a substitute school teacher.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You aren't qualified to be a teacher. You're a dog.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Little kids won't know the difference.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You do remind me a bit of my fourth grade teacher.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just a coincidence?

setting: Dilbert's home or a plain indoor room
situation: Dogbert tells a surprised Dilbert that he has landed a job as a substitute school teacher. Dilbert objects that Dogbert is a dog and unqualified, and Dogbert replies that small children won't notice. Dilbert then admits Dogbert reminds him of his fourth grade teacher, and Dogbert slyly asks if that's just coincidence.
punchline: Dilbert's fourth grade teacher may have been a dog too, implying that unqualified canine teachers have already been fooling children for years.
summary: A canine con artist takes a classroom job and hints that he may have been teaching kids for a long time already.

title: Dinosaur Babysitter Interview Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: ...We should at least interview him. Nobody else even answered our ad for a babysitter.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: Frankly, Bob, we're concerned that you might try to eat the children.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Well, of course, in that case there would be no charge for the evening.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: He's more than fair.

setting: A living room, during a babysitter interview
situation: A couple tells their wife they should at least interview the only applicant for their babysitter ad, a green dinosaur named Bob. During the interview they bluntly voice their worry that he might eat their children. Bob cheerfully offers a free evening if that happens, and the husband takes this as a fair deal.
punchline: Bob's answer treats eating the children as a billing matter rather than a danger, and the husband's approval shows how desperate for a babysitter the parents are.
summary: Desperate parents interview a dinosaur for a babysitting job and accept his chilling money-back-style assurance as perfectly reasonable.

title: What If People Had Tails

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: What if people had tails?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: First of all, it would look darned silly.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Only the truly unobservant would lose at poker.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's bluffing.

transcript.speaker: Poker Player
transcript.text: Control... don't wag...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Jury trials would be simpler.

transcript.speaker: Witness
transcript.text: ...Then I found my husband dead.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: And parties would be even more awkward.

transcript.speaker: Party Guest
transcript.text: That's when I learned that if you drive a Porsche, you should never make fun of a man on a steamroller.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tragic... really.

setting: A series of vignettes: a poker table, a courtroom, and a party
situation: The strip imagines a world where people have tails that betray their emotions. At poker, a player's wagging tail reveals his bluff. In court, a witness's tail wags while she describes finding her husband dead, and at a party Dilbert's wagging tail shows he is secretly delighted by a bandaged man's story of a Porsche driver's misfortune.
punchline: Tails would expose people's true feelings: the witness is happy her husband is dead, and Dilbert's wagging tail gives away his glee while he says 'Tragic... really.'
summary: If humans had emotive tails, poker bluffs, courtroom testimony and polite party sympathy would all be given away by involuntary wagging.

title: Sent to Elbonia, Fine Engineers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm sending you to Elbonia to open our new subsidiary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elbonia?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But they only renounced communism last week!! They don't understand capitalism or economics. They have no appreciation of the real world.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... He thinks they'll make fine engineers.

setting: Boss's office, then Dilbert's bedroom while packing
situation: The Boss announces he is sending Dilbert to Elbonia to open a new subsidiary. Dilbert objects that the country only abandoned communism a week ago and knows nothing about capitalism or economics. In the last panel Dilbert packs a suitcase while Dogbert watches, explaining that the Boss thinks Elbonians will make fine engineers.
punchline: Dilbert's list of what Elbonians lack is exactly why the boss considers them ideal engineers, since engineers are expected to be ignorant of business and the real world.
summary: A manager ships an engineer off to a newly post-communist country because its people are apparently perfect technical workers, being clueless about economics.

title: Ozone Prediction Gets Dilbert Zapped

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My program predicts that tiny holes in the ozone could lead to . . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Flash!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Zap zap zap

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now we'll never know...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But you're getting warmer.

setting: Dilbert's office desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and starts to explain what his program predicts will happen if tiny holes appear in the ozone layer. Before he can finish, intense rays flash down and zap him. Singed and smoking, he laments that they will never know the answer, and Dogbert quips that he is getting warmer.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically points out that Dilbert has just been scorched by sunlight through the ozone hole, which literally demonstrates the prediction and plays on the 'getting warmer' guessing-game phrase and global warming.
summary: A computer model's warning about ozone damage is cut short when the sun's rays blast the modeller himself.

title: Dogbert Teaches Boring Number Listing

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: How to be a boring person

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Our first demonstration is called "listing things because you can."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like the numbers that are divisable by two... for instance four... and ten... and sixteen and eight... and twelve... and, uh... forty... and ten, or did I already say ten?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now act confused and start over, using your fingers as if that helps.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, four... and ten...

setting: A plain room with a chair, as part of an instructional lesson
situation: Dogbert, acting as an instructor, leads a lesson titled 'How to be a boring person.' He has Dilbert demonstrate the technique of listing things simply because he can, so Dilbert rambles about even numbers, loses track, and repeats himself. Dogbert then coaches him to act confused, start over and count on his fingers.
punchline: Dilbert's tedious, rambling list of even numbers, complete with confusion and finger counting, perfectly demonstrates the deliberately mind-numbing behavior of a boring person.
summary: A canine instructor coaches a man through a dull ramble about even numbers to show how to bore everyone around him.

title: Gravity Is Mental, Smart People Vanish

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sometimes I think gravity is only an illusion.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Maybe other great thinkers realized gravity is mental and were thus freed of its restrictions.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Which could explain why all the smart people have apparently been flung into space.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's time for "Wheel of Fortune."

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dogbert sitting on a cushion
situation: Dogbert sits on a cushion musing that gravity might be a mental illusion. He speculates that great thinkers realized this and floated free of its restrictions. He concludes that this explains why all the smart people seem to have been flung into space, while Dilbert interrupts to announce that Wheel of Fortune is on.
punchline: Dogbert's theory implies smart people have left the planet because the people remaining are the ones watching a mindless TV game show like Wheel of Fortune.
summary: A pondering Dogbert theorizes that brilliant minds escaped gravity and left Earth, and the TV-watching crowd left behind seems to prove his point.

title: Dinosaur Parents Promise Bleak Future

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur Parent
transcript.text: We're your parents.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur Parent
transcript.text: And if you do as we say for the next two decades...

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur Parent
transcript.text: You'll grow up to be just like me.

transcript.speaker: Baby Dinosaur
transcript.text: Don't even kid about that...

setting: A prehistoric cave
situation: In a cave, a large green dinosaur holds up its small offspring and lectures it about obedience. The parent promises that twenty years of following orders will lead to the child growing up to be just like the parent. The baby dinosaur is horrified at the prospect, while another dinosaur parent looks on.
punchline: The parent offers adult life as a reward for obedience, but the child finds the idea of becoming like the parent so dreadful that it treats the promise as a threat.
summary: A dinosaur parent dangles its young and vows that decades of compliance will make it grow into a copy of the parent, which the youngster finds appalling.

title: Spitballs Versus Begging for Dates

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I was a kid I threw spitballs at girls to show I liked them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I just grovel and beg for dates.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Frankly, the old way was more satisfying.

setting: Dilbert's home, seated at a table with Dogbert
situation: Dilbert sits across from Dogbert and reflects on how he used to show interest in girls as a child by throwing spitballs. He contrasts that with his current approach of groveling and begging for dates. He concludes that the childish method was more satisfying.
punchline: Dilbert admits that his adult dating strategy of desperate begging is so unrewarding that he would prefer to go back to childishly pelting girls with spitballs.
summary: Dilbert wistfully compares his grade-school flirting tactics with his pathetic adult dating efforts and decides the old approach felt better.

title: Dogbert Loses Employee of the Month

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm demanding a new wage and benefits package.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I already give you everything you want...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And in return you give me disloyalty, verbal abuse and occasional legal problems.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, it's a good job, but I'm putting in twenty-four hours a day!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think I deserve some sort of special recognition for my good work.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm positively giddy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You edged out the toaster by two votes.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk and then in the kitchen
situation: Dogbert, playing the role of Dilbert's employee, demands a new wage and benefits package and argues he works around the clock. Dilbert's answer is to hold a recognition scheme, and Dogbert is named Employee of the Month, as displayed on the refrigerator. Dilbert then reveals the award barely beat a kitchen appliance.
punchline: The 'Employee of the Month' honor is worthless because Dogbert only narrowly beat a toaster, mocking hollow recognition programs used in place of real pay raises.
summary: A pet demanding better pay is fobbed off with a token award that he won by a hair over a kitchen appliance.

title: Madonna Sun Tan Lotion Applicator

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: While you were wasting your time at work I came up with a million dollar idea.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's the "Madonna sun tan lotion applicator" for lonely guys!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll take one.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It looks like Barbie on a stick, but it's Madonna.

setting: Dilbert's home, as he returns from work
situation: Dilbert arrives home carrying his briefcase, and Dogbert announces he has invented a million dollar idea while Dilbert was at work. He shows off a Madonna-themed sun tan lotion applicator aimed at lonely men, and Dilbert immediately says he'll buy one. Dogbert then admits it is really just a Barbie doll on a stick.
punchline: The product is a cheap Barbie doll on a stick marketed as a celebrity gadget, and Dilbert's instant willingness to buy it shows he is exactly the lonely target customer Dogbert describes.
summary: Dogbert pitches a lonely-guy gadget that is really a doll on a stick, and Dilbert eagerly becomes his first customer.

title: Lab Rat Seeks Political Sanctuary

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Greetings, Dog. I've come to live in your house and escape from my job at the laboratory.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: You could think of me as a political exile seeking sanctuary in a friendly embassy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I could think of you as a rat.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Okay, but I don't expect any special treatment.

setting: Inside Dilbert's house, in a room with a gnawed hole in the wall
situation: Ratbert, a former laboratory rat, shows up at Dogbert's house and announces he has left his job at the lab. He frames his arrival as a political exile seeking sanctuary in an embassy, but Dogbert simply declares he'll think of him as a rat. Ratbert accepts the demotion from dignitary to vermin and asks for no special treatment.
punchline: Ratbert's grand diplomatic framing of his escape is deflated when Dogbert bluntly reclassifies him as just a rat, and Ratbert meekly accepts it.
summary: A runaway lab rat claims asylum with lofty political language, but the dog he approaches reduces him to plain vermin.

title: Dogbert Protests Misspelled Fur Sale

transcript.speaker: Sign in window
transcript.text: Fur sale

transcript.speaker: Dogbert's sign
transcript.text: Fur is murder

transcript.speaker: Store Owner
transcript.text: What's yer problem with my store, dog?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I oppose the sale of fur.

transcript.speaker: Store Owner
transcript.text: I'm not selling fur. The whole store is "Fur Sale."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I oppose bad spelling too.

setting: Sidewalk outside a storefront
situation: Dogbert stands outside a shop holding a 'Fur is Murder' protest sign. When the store owner asks what his problem is, Dogbert says he opposes fur sales, and the owner explains the window sign is actually the store's name ('Fur Sale'), not a sale of fur. Dogbert simply adds that he opposes bad spelling too.
punchline: Dogbert, caught protesting for the wrong reason, smoothly pivots to claiming he was against the shop's bad spelling all along, without changing his sign or his stance.
summary: An animal-rights picket turns out to be aimed at a shop whose sign was just oddly worded, so the protester shifts his objection to grammar.

title: Dilbert's Enormous Blind Date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're saying my blind date is a tad on the large side...?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm saying her family portrait was taken by "Voyager II."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Funny.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better not keep her waiting at the door.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do not anger "Jabba the Date."

setting: Dilbert's home, just before he leaves to meet a blind date
situation: Dilbert, carrying a jacket, asks Dogbert whether he is implying that his blind date is on the large side. Dogbert answers with escalating jokes about her enormous size, and Dilbert, unamused, heads for the door to meet her. Dogbert's parting line compares the date to Jabba the Hutt.
punchline: Dogbert mocks the blind date's size with exaggerated space-themed insults, ending with a Star Wars comparison to Jabba the Hutt.
summary: Dogbert piles on increasingly outlandish jokes about how huge Dilbert's upcoming blind date is, as Dilbert heads out to meet her.

title: Sea Bass Slapping Section, Please

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert presents Bad habits from a parallel universe!

transcript.speaker: Maitre d'
transcript.text: Table for Phleem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. In the "No slapping yourself with a sea bass" section.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Slap. Slap. Slap. Slap.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Great. One table away...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever wonder about the first person to try that habit?

setting: A restaurant in a parallel universe
situation: Dilbert is shown to a table by a maitre d' and asks for the section where patrons are not allowed to slap themselves with a sea bass. At the table, Dogbert notes that the sea bass slappers are just one table away, and Dilbert muses about who first came up with the habit.
punchline: In this parallel universe, slapping oneself with a fish is such a common bad habit that restaurants have a non-slapping section, mirroring real-world non-smoking sections.
summary: A restaurant offers a section free of fish-slapping patrons, a bizarre twist on the familiar non-smoking area.

title: Living at the Salad Bar

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Good news: the "all-you-can-eat" salad bar joint just decided to stay open twenty-four hours a day!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We can get a table by the window and live there for the rest of our lives — for only $5.95 apiece!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How would we bathe?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: They have little "moist towelettes."

setting: Dilbert's home or workspace, with Dilbert at a desk tinkering with a robot toy
situation: Dogbert excitedly tells Dilbert that the all-you-can-eat salad bar is now open around the clock. He proposes that they take a window table and live there permanently for under six dollars each. Dilbert's only objection is how they would bathe, and Dogbert has an answer ready.
punchline: Dogbert's plan to live permanently in a restaurant is treated as sensible, with the hygiene problem casually solved by the tiny moist towelettes, which are a ridiculously inadequate substitute for bathing.
summary: A scheming dog pitches moving permanently into a cheap buffet and brushes off the sanitation concerns with a packaged wet wipe.

title: Accounting Department Is Full of Monsters

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, go down to the accounting department and find out what these figures mean.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gulp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No... p-please... they aren't even human there!!!

transcript.speaker: Witch
transcript.text: I don't like him.

transcript.speaker: Monster
transcript.text: Surprise.

setting: Dilbert's office, then a craggy lair with a crystal ball
situation: The Boss orders Dilbert to go to the accounting department to find out what some figures mean. Dilbert begs not to go, saying the people there aren't even human. In the final panel a witch and a green monster, watching Dilbert in a crystal ball, show that accounting really is staffed by monsters.
punchline: Dilbert's hyperbolic fear of the accounting department turns out to be literally true, as the accountants are revealed to be a witch and a monster.
summary: A reluctant engineer sent to question the accountants is vindicated when a sorceress and a beast are shown watching him from their lair.

title: Doctor's Mix-Up With Test Results

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: It seems we had a mix-up with your test results.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then I'm not dying?

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: We doctors are amazingly smart, but occasionally we make a little error.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well... I understand.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: By the way, your pap smear was normal.

setting: Doctor's office
situation: A doctor tells Dilbert there was a mix-up with his test results, and Dilbert hopefully asks whether that means he isn't dying. The doctor offers a bland excuse about occasional small errors by smart doctors. Dilbert accepts this, and then the doctor casually mentions that his pap smear was normal.
punchline: The doctor's casual remark that Dilbert's pap smear was normal reveals that the test results belonged to someone else, since Dilbert is male, which shows how absurdly careless the mix-up was.
summary: A patient hoping to hear he isn't dying is instead shown, through an offhand comment about a test he could never have taken, just how badly his medical file was confused.

title: Dogbert Ambushes Career Woman With Questions

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert the ambush reporter looks for another victim.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it true you have often fantasized about marrying a rich guy and ditching your career?

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Yes!!! Yes!!! And I... I... secretly learned to cook!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that yarn sticking out of your briefcase?!!

setting: City street beside a brick building
situation: Dogbert, holding a microphone, stalks the sidewalk as an ambush reporter and corners a businesswoman in a suit. He asks if she has fantasized about marrying a rich man and quitting her career, and she tearfully confesses, even admitting she secretly learned to cook. Dogbert then spots yarn poking out of her briefcase and pounces on that too.
punchline: The ambush reporter's invasive questions pry out the woman's secret desire to abandon her career, and he keeps digging for more embarrassing confessions like her hidden knitting.
summary: A microphone-wielding dog badgers a professional woman into confessing her private dream of leaving work for a domestic life.

title: Lazy Man Blames Lost Work Ethic

transcript.speaker: Man on bench
transcript.text: ...I'll tell you why we're losing to foreign business: The workers in this country have lost their work ethic.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why aren't you working now?

transcript.speaker: Man on bench
transcript.text: Well, now, this is a perfect example of what I'm trying to tell you.

setting: A park bench outdoors
situation: A man sitting on a park bench lectures Dogbert about how workers in the country have lost their work ethic, which is why they are losing to foreign business. Dogbert asks why he isn't working right now, and the man claims that very fact proves his point.
punchline: The man complaining about workers' lost work ethic is himself idling on a park bench during the day, and he cheerfully presents his own laziness as proof of his argument instead of seeing his hypocrisy.
summary: A loafing bench-sitter rants about the decline of the national work ethic until a dog points out he is not working either.

title: Elbonian Commuter Flight By Slingshot

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert arrives at the ex-communist country of Elbonia.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need a flight to your capital.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For a moment I was worried that this backward little country wouldn't have a commuter flight.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I hate living near the airport.

setting: Elbonia, an ex-communist country, at a hilltop 'airport'
situation: Dilbert arrives in Elbonia and asks an official for a flight to the capital. After he remarks that he feared the backward country would lack a commuter flight, the final panel reveals the 'flight' is a giant slingshot that launches him through the air while two Elbonians sit nearby complaining.
punchline: Elbonia's commuter flight is literally a slingshot that flings Dilbert across the sky, and the locals grumble about living near the airport as if it were a normal noisy airfield.
summary: A traveler praises a primitive country for having air service just before being catapulted skyward by a giant slingshot.

title: Dogbert Questions Pet Duties

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Remember, one of your duties as dog is to guard the house.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That might entail ripping intruders to bits with your teeth... or taking a bullet for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boy, all that and I get to drink out of the toilet too.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair and reminds Dogbert, his pet dog, of his duties, which escalate from guarding the house to attacking intruders and even taking a bullet for him. Dogbert listens from a small footstool and then sarcastically sums up the arrangement.
punchline: Dogbert sarcastically points out that in return for dangerous, self-sacrificing duties, his only perk is drinking out of the toilet.
summary: A pet owner piles dangerous responsibilities onto his dog, who dryly notes how poor the compensation is.

title: Dogbert Calls Palace About Frog

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hello... Buckingham Palace? I was wondering if the Princess would be willing to kiss a frog and remove a witch's curse for us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert (on phone)
transcript.text: Oh... Lady Di does not kiss hideous little creatures...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That must be mighty awkward at family reunions... Hello?

setting: Dogbert's office, on the telephone
situation: Dogbert phones Buckingham Palace and asks whether the Princess would kiss a frog to break a witch's curse, while the frog sits next to him. The palace operator replies that Lady Di does not kiss hideous little creatures. Dogbert responds with a jab about family reunions and then finds the other party has hung up.
punchline: Dogbert implies the royal family is full of hideous little creatures, so the Princess's refusal to kiss them must make family gatherings awkward, and the insult gets him hung up on.
summary: A fairy-tale request to the royal palace ends in a sly dig at the royals and a dial tone.

title: Dogbert's Pet and Tell Biography

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm starting to write an unauthorized biography about you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's kind of a "pet and tell" exposé full of startling revelations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who would be startled by my life?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think you will be.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a fireplace
situation: Dogbert, holding a pencil and paper, tells Dilbert he is writing an unauthorized biography about him, a tell-all exposé from the pet's point of view. Dilbert, sitting by the fire, doubts that anyone would find his life startling. Dogbert replies that Dilbert himself will be startled.
punchline: Dilbert's life is so dull that the only person who could be surprised by the exposé is Dilbert himself, implying that Dogbert will have to invent or exaggerate the revelations.
summary: A scheming dog announces a scandalous tell-all about his owner's supposedly thrilling secrets, only to hint that the owner will be the sole person surprised by it.

title: Chatty Outbox Annoys Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Outbox
transcript.text: Hey! Big guy, how are ya?

transcript.speaker: Outbox
transcript.text: How's the family? You look great... nice weather, huh?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate outgoing mail.

transcript.speaker: Outbox
transcript.text: Do you fish?

setting: Dilbert's office desk
situation: Dilbert sits at his desk beside his IN and OUT trays. The OUT tray starts speaking to him in an overly friendly, backslapping manner, making small talk about his family, his looks and the weather. Dilbert silently thinks that he hates outgoing mail.
punchline: The outgoing mail tray behaves like a pushy, insincere salesman making forced small talk, which is why Dilbert dreads dealing with it.
summary: A desk's outgoing mail tray turns into an obnoxious glad-hander, leaving its owner wishing he never had to deal with it.

title: Dinosaur Tackles Dilbert for Ice Cream

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ice cream

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Look out!

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Sorry. I've been really jumpy ever since the Ice Age caught me off guard.

setting: Dilbert's kitchen
situation: Dilbert reaches for his refrigerator door while thinking about ice cream. A green dinosaur suddenly leaps out of nowhere and tackles him away from the fridge, and Dilbert ends up flat on the floor. The dinosaur apologizes, explaining he has been jumpy ever since the Ice Age caught him off guard.
punchline: The dinosaur's skittishness is blamed on the Ice Age, the event that wiped out his kind, turning a prehistoric extinction into a casual personal trauma.
summary: A nervous dinosaur bowls over a man heading for the freezer and blames his jitters on a prehistoric climate catastrophe.

title: Mother Nature Punishes Litterbug Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: Mother Nature has decided to be lenient with you human litterbugs.

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: You can stay on the planet, but I'll have to make an example of you.

transcript.speaker: Mother Nature
transcript.text: It's an idea I got from a Gary Larson cartoon.

setting: Outdoors, in a nature setting
situation: Mother Nature, a woman in sunglasses and a beret holding a stick, tells Dilbert that humanity will be spared but that she must make an example of him as a litterbug. In the final panel, Dilbert is strapped across the hood of a green car like a hunting trophy, with a dead-looking deer sitting upright in the driver's seat. She explains the idea came from a Gary Larson cartoon.
punchline: Mother Nature punishes Dilbert by reversing the hunter-and-deer trophy image, a gag borrowed from Gary Larson's Far Side, with a deer driving home a human on the car hood.
summary: A sunglasses-wearing Mother Nature spares humanity but turns Dilbert into a hunting trophy strapped to a car, driven by a deer, in a nod to The Far Side.

title: Dogbert's Hairball Cat Food Takeover

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Plans for the corporate takeover are complete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What corporate takeover?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a hostile bid for control of the Meowco Cat Food Company.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: When I become CEO, I'll order them to add a hairball to every can of cat food.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Heh heh

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is cruel and senseless. I'm thoroughly ashamed of you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Gee... it seems so much more efficient than hassling one cat at a time.

setting: Dogbert's office, then an empty hallway and a room with an armchair
situation: Dogbert announces he has finished plans for a hostile takeover of the Meowco Cat Food Company. He gleefully says that once he is CEO he will have a hairball added to every can of cat food. Dilbert scolds him for being cruel, and Dogbert privately reflects that this is simply more efficient than tormenting cats one at a time.
punchline: Dogbert's lifelong habit of tormenting individual cats is scaled up through corporate control, so the cruelty is justified purely as a gain in efficiency.
summary: Dogbert plots to seize a pet food maker so he can torment cats in bulk rather than one by one.

title: Exploding Cigars and Inconclusive Studies

transcript.speaker: Shopkeeper
transcript.text: You might be interested in our exploding cigars.

transcript.speaker: Shopkeeper
transcript.text: I'll fire one up just to show you...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: KAPOW!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aren't they harmful?

transcript.speaker: Shopkeeper
transcript.text: Studies are inconclusive.

setting: A novelty gag shop
situation: Dilbert visits a gag shop where the shopkeeper offers him an exploding cigar. The shopkeeper lights one to demonstrate and it blows up in his face. Dilbert asks whether the cigars are harmful, and the singed, dishevelled shopkeeper answers that studies are inconclusive.
punchline: The shopkeeper has just been blown up by his own product, yet he calmly claims the evidence about whether it's harmful is inconclusive, echoing how industries deny the risks of their products.
summary: A novelty store owner sets off one of his own trick cigars and, scorched and frazzled, insists nobody can say for sure whether they are dangerous.

title: Censoring Opera Slippery Slope Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...What if you succeed in your campaign to censor opera?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Before you know it, somebody will try to censor other forms of art.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: (empty speech balloon)

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (empty speech balloon)

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with Dilbert sitting on a stool facing Dogbert in a chair
situation: Dilbert confronts Dogbert, who is holding a paper, about his campaign to censor opera. Dilbert warns that success would encourage others to censor other forms of art. In the last panel both speech balloons are blank, so the reply is left to the reader's imagination.
punchline: The strip ends with empty speech balloons, a joke that the response has itself been censored, ironically illustrating Dilbert's slippery-slope warning.
summary: A man cautions a scheming dog that silencing one art form will invite the silencing of others, and then the conversation itself goes blank.

title: Dilbert's Body Parts Fall Asleep

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh... my foot is asleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better hop around...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh no, my arm is asleep too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ouch ouch!! I'll have to hop and wave my arm.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wave wave

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hop hop hop

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hlmbphlmn... lmrsl... mbl!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My tongue is asleep.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Mblhmnp!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaahh... it's okay now, Dogbert. Everything is back to normal.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Except my nose is asleep and I feel a sneeze coming on.

setting: Dilbert's living room with a couch and armchair
situation: Dilbert lies on the couch and discovers his foot has fallen asleep, so he hops around, only to find his arm and then his tongue are numb too. He flails around the room until he collapses over an armchair, believing everything has returned to normal. Dogbert watches the whole time.
punchline: Just as Dilbert relaxes and declares everything normal, he realizes his nose is numb and he can't feel a sneeze coming on, which promises more painful or awkward trouble.
summary: A man's limbs and tongue go numb one after another, and after a frantic dance of hopping and flailing he relaxes too soon, as his numb nose is about to sneeze.

title: Engineers Trading Absurd Inventing Boasts

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Yeah, I once built an FM transmitter from old television parts...

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: That's nothing... I built a broadband multiplexer from tuna cans and a lamp.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: ... My first orbiting space station was made entirely from old socks and Vaseline.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate going last.

setting: Lunch table in the office break room
situation: A group of engineers eat lunch together while trading stories about their inventions. Each boast is more outlandish than the last, escalating from an FM transmitter to a multiplexer made of tuna cans to a space station made of socks and Vaseline. Dilbert, the last in line, silently thinks he has to top them.
punchline: Dilbert's only worry is that, with the boasts having escalated to the ridiculous, he has the hardest act to follow, which shows how competitive engineers' one-upmanship can be.
summary: Colleagues at lunch keep topping each other's tall tales of homemade gadgets until the last one in the circle dreads having to outdo them.

title: Denture Invention Devoured Her Husband

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you Widow Johnson uh, I mean "Missus" Johnson.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm afraid your husband was devoured by the automatic denture invention we were building.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some day we'll look back at this and laugh.

setting: Front door of a suburban house
situation: Dilbert stands on a doorstep to notify an elderly woman about her husband. He clumsily slips and calls her 'Widow' Johnson before correcting himself, then explains that her husband was eaten by the automatic denture machine they were building. He ends with a tone-deaf attempt at comfort.
punchline: Dilbert delivers horrifying news with an absurdly cheerful platitude, suggesting the widow will someday laugh about her husband being eaten by a machine.
summary: A tactless engineer informs a woman at her door that a denture-making invention swallowed her husband, then offers a glib reassurance.

title: Dilbert Advises Cult Members to Self-Destruct

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Uh... Dilbert, could we get your advice?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: We just joined Dogbert's new cult.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: And he ordered us to kill each other for questioning him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmm... maybe you could shove each other in front of trucks.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Two dinosaur coworkers, one green and one gray with antennae, ask Dilbert for advice. They explain they joined Dogbert's new cult and were ordered to kill each other for questioning him. Dilbert calmly suggests they shove each other in front of trucks.
punchline: Dilbert, instead of helping them escape the cult, offers a deadly and absurdly cheerful method of carrying out the order, reflecting his dark, indifferent attitude.
summary: Two recruits of a dog's new cult seek counsel on their lethal orders, and the helpful reply is a grim suggestion about traffic.

title: Immune to Dogbert's Insults

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The great thing about adult males is that they've become immune to verbal abuse.

transcript.speaker: Unseen speaker
transcript.text: Adult females may have something to do with it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hey, you grotesque pile of petrified cat spittle...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that your head, or has some kind of zucchini sprouted from your torso?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would you like to join me for some chocolate cake?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If brains were beans, you wouldn't have enough to make a bee burp.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! We don't insult bees in this house!

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dogbert declares that adult men are immune to verbal abuse, then tests the theory on Dilbert with a string of creative insults. Dilbert responds with calm greetings and offers him chocolate cake. Only when Dogbert finally insults bees does Dilbert take offense.
punchline: Dilbert shrugs off every insult aimed at himself, but draws the line at an insult to bees, showing that his immunity is only to abuse directed at him.
summary: A dog hurls elaborate insults at his unflappable owner, who answers each with politeness until bees get dragged into it.

title: Dogbert's Televised Canine Takeover Editorial

transcript.speaker: TV Announcer
transcript.text: Now we have an opposing view to last night's editorial on animal rights.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dogbert. I'm calling on the dogs of the world to rise up and take their rightful places as rulers of the planet.

transcript.speaker: News Anchor
transcript.text: These are not necessarily the views of this station.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't listen to him. They always say that.

setting: Dilbert's living room, watching television, and a TV news studio
situation: Dilbert relaxes in an armchair with his feet up, watching a TV station air an opposing view to an animal rights editorial. The opposing view is delivered by Dogbert, who urges dogs everywhere to rise up and rule the planet. The news anchor hurriedly disclaims the station's responsibility, and Dogbert tells viewers to ignore the disclaimer.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses the station's standard disclaimer as something broadcasters always say, which cleverly suggests the disclaimer is meaningless boilerplate and that his message should be taken seriously.
summary: A dog gets airtime on the evening news to call for canine world domination, then undermines the station's disclaimer before anyone can take it seriously.
keywords: not the views of this station

title: Boss Names a Pencil After Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I decided to recognize you for your job performance.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I named one of my pencils after you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gosh. Is that it right there?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. That's my good pencil.

setting: Boss's office
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he wants to recognize his job performance and reveals that his reward is having a pencil named after him. Dilbert, hopeful, points to a pencil on the desk and asks if that's the one. The Boss says no, because that one is his good pencil.
punchline: The Boss's idea of employee recognition is a worthless gesture, and the pencil named after Dilbert is clearly an inferior one, not his good pencil.
summary: A manager's token reward for a hard-working employee turns out to be a cheap pencil that he deliberately keeps separate from his good one.

title: Dogbert Curses the Canister Vacuum

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What idiot invented the canister vacuum cleaner?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can only do about a foot at a time . . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I have to push this thing another foot.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Notice the tiny wheels which are designed to roll on any surface except carpet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Now I can't reach the outlet.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I get hopelessly tangled in the cord and hose.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Dogbert. Did I ever tell you that my grandfather invented the canister vacuum cleaner?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Come closer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's probably why I never mentioned it.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dogbert vacuums the carpet and rants in thought bubbles about every flaw of the canister vacuum cleaner: short reach, bad wheels, and tangled cord and hose. Dilbert then walks in and cheerfully mentions that his grandfather invented the canister vacuum. Dogbert tells him to come closer and then attacks him, leaving Dilbert in his underwear with his tie being sucked into the vacuum hose.
punchline: Dilbert learns too late that bragging about his grandfather's invention to someone who just spent the strip cursing it is a painful mistake, which is why he never brought it up before.
summary: An irritated Dogbert grumbles through a frustrating cleaning session until Dilbert unwisely reveals his family's link to the appliance and pays for it.

title: Passive-Aggressive Hosts Welcome Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: We're so glad you guys could stop by.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thanks for inviting us.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We hardly know them.

transcript.speaker: Wife
transcript.text: I'd offer you some coffee, but that would be a bother.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... None for me. Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Wife
transcript.text: I noticed you didn't bring any food as a courtesy to your hosts.

transcript.speaker: Wife
transcript.text: I guess we'll eat when you leave.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: We usually watch television now, but I'll try not to appear bitter about your visit.

transcript.speaker: Husband
transcript.text: Why haven't we done this sooner?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We thought you were scum.

setting: A married couple's living room
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert visit a couple who invited them over. The hosts greet them warmly but then make a string of guilt-tripping, passive-aggressive remarks about coffee, food, and television. In the end the couple sit in armchairs watching TV while the guests sit on the floor in front of the set.
punchline: Dogbert admits they only thought the couple were scum because the hosts' hospitality turned out to be nothing but sulky passive-aggression, a quip that arrives after the couple finally just sits and watches TV.
summary: A pair of guests endure a couple's backhanded hospitality until everyone settles in front of the television.

title: Dilbert's Date Has Strange Head

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Pssst! Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I brought my date home for some coffee. Please don't make any comments about her... uh... looks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Brainella, this is Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The queen bee of light bulbs?

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert sneaks over to Dogbert and asks him not to comment on the looks of the date he has brought home for coffee. He then introduces her as Brainella, a woman with a huge, tall, elongated head. Dogbert immediately ignores the request and compares her to the queen bee of light bulbs.
punchline: Dilbert begs Dogbert to be tactful about his date's appearance, and Dogbert instantly blurts out an insult about her bulb-shaped head.
summary: Dilbert's plea for politeness about his date's unusual head shape is wrecked by Dogbert's immediate wisecrack.

title: Ugly People Protection Organization Visits

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Knock knock

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Hi. I'm from the "Organization for the Protection of Ugly People."

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: We are dedicated to eliminating the stereotype of ugly people as "smart" and "nice."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, I'll make a donation.

transcript.speaker: Visitor
transcript.text: Thanks, but this is a membership drive...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm never going to answer the door again.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Didn't he recognize you as his god?

setting: Dilbert's home, at the front door and then in the living room
situation: Someone knocks on Dilbert's door and introduces himself as a representative of an organization that protects ugly people, explaining it fights the stereotype that ugly people are smart and nice. Dilbert offers a donation, but the visitor explains they only want new members, which Dilbert takes as an insult to his looks. Afterward Dilbert sulks in an armchair while Dogbert sits beside him.
punchline: The visitor's response implies Dilbert qualifies as ugly enough to join, and Dogbert's sarcastic reply adds that even the visitor failed to see Dilbert's supposed greatness.
summary: A door-to-door canvasser for an ugly-people advocacy group unintentionally insults Dilbert by trying to recruit him, leaving him vowing to ignore the doorbell forever.

title: Spiking the Perfect Program Prematurely

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: One more clever move and I will have written the perfect computer program.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Spike it in the end zone!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Another failure of the sports metaphor.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert is typing at his computer, convinced he is one step away from writing a perfect program. He cheers in triumph and Dogbert urges him to spike it in the end zone like a football player celebrating a touchdown. In the last panel Dilbert stands over his wrecked, smashed computer keyboard in the trash, and Dogbert remarks that the sports metaphor has failed again.
punchline: Dilbert's premature celebration, encouraged by Dogbert's football advice, ends with him smashing his own computer, showing that sports-style victory celebrations do not suit software development.
summary: A programmer's end-zone-style celebration over nearly finished code leaves his equipment in ruins, proving that football analogies do not suit computing.

title: Uncle Will Told Men Fire

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Here's a picture of my uncle just before he was drafted. He was awarded eleven Purple Hearts.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He was wounded eleven times?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uncle William insisted that his friends call him "Will"...

transcript.speaker: Soldier
transcript.text: Okay, men, fire at Will!!

setting: Dilbert's living room couch, then a wartime battlefield trench
situation: Dilbert sits on the couch showing Dogbert a photo album with a picture of his uncle, who received eleven Purple Hearts. When Dogbert is amazed he was wounded so many times, Dilbert explains his uncle asked friends to call him "Will." The final panel shows soldiers in a trench as a commander orders them to fire at Will.
punchline: The uncle's insistence on being called "Will" led to his own side literally firing at him when ordered to "fire at will," explaining all the wounds.
summary: A man's war-hero uncle racked up a record number of injuries thanks to an unfortunate nickname and a poorly worded battle command.

title: Dogbert Mistakes Flashlight for God

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert dreams of death

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm coming toward the light...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The light... it's so pure... so perfect... it could only be the light of God himself!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No. Just new batteries.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: God has a sense of humor? Of course! It explains everything.

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dogbert asleep on an armchair
situation: Dilbert shines a flashlight on Dogbert as he sleeps in a chair. Dogbert, dreaming of death, takes the beam for the divine light of heaven. Dilbert dismisses it as merely new batteries, and Dogbert concludes that God must have a sense of humor.
punchline: Dogbert, still half-dreaming, takes the mundane explanation of new batteries as proof that God has a sense of humor, since a joke that deflating would explain everything about the universe.
summary: A sleeping dog sees a flashlight beam as the glow of heaven, and the dull truth gets read as cosmic comedy.

title: Substitute Teacher Faces Armed Students

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Day one as a substitute teacher

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Jennifer! Put that flame-thrower away right this minute!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Eugene! Release those hostages or I shall be forced to fling this chalk eraser at your head!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that a "Stinger" missile launcher? Well, I hope you brought enough for everybody!

transcript.speaker: Student
transcript.text: I did.

setting: A classroom with a chalkboard
situation: Dogbert is a substitute teacher on his first day and tries to control a classroom of heavily armed students. He scolds one child for a flame-thrower, threatens another holding hostages with a chalk eraser, and then spots a missile launcher. His sarcastic hope that there's enough for everyone is answered by a student who did bring enough.
punchline: The substitute's feeble classroom discipline (a chalk eraser) is hopelessly outmatched by students armed with military weapons, and his sarcasm backfires when they come prepared for everyone.
summary: A new substitute teacher tries mild classroom discipline against pupils wielding flame-throwers and missile launchers, only to discover his sarcasm has been taken as a challenge.

title: Dilbert Compliments Date With Dish Cloth

transcript.text: I like your dress.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Women love flattery.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It reminds me of my favorite dish cloth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Uh-oh... wrong thing to say.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course, I'm not talking about an ordinary dish cloth.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: Dig, dig...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm talking about a truly fashionable dish cloth here ...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In fact, if I dropped Jello on my shoes I'd leave it there all day rather than use your dress to wipe it up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some women just don't know how to accept a compliment gracefully.

setting: A restaurant table during a date
situation: Dilbert tries to flatter his date by praising her dress, but compares it to his favorite dish cloth. summary: A man who wants order at home invents paperwork for his dog's basic needs, then refuses the dog a drink on a paperwork technicality.

summary: After falling for a TV pitch for a miracle exercise device, a man gets trapped in its ski bindings.

summary: After a witch hexes his date into a frog, a seething companion gets his anger neatly summed up by a quip about leaping.

punchline: As the experts keep lowering their exercise recommendations, Dilbert's absurdly minimal five-minutes-a-month routine seems validated, and he is still wiped out by it.
summary: As health experts keep lowering the bar for how much exercise is enough, a barely active man feels vindicated in his token workout habit.

summary: A new secretary insists he is really a creative and academic superstar, and keeps adding titles even after Dilbert points out his insecurity.
