situation: Dilbert gently bumps another car and checks for damage, only to find the other driver folded upside down in the front seat. The man threatens to sue and later tells the court he can never work again. Under questioning he admits he was a circus contortionist.
punchline: The injured plaintiff's job as a contortionist explains his odd position, and his closing line about being 'flexible' on the settlement is a pun on his profession.
summary: A man twisted into a pretzel after a tiny collision sues the driver who tapped him, and his contortionist career makes his settlement terms a pun.

title: Mom's Danger Warning Backfires

transcript.speaker: Mother Dinosaur
transcript.text: Little dinosaurs must listen to their mothers.

transcript.speaker: Little Dinosaur
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Mother Dinosaur
transcript.text: Uh... Because older dinosaurs have experience... we know how to avoid danger.

transcript.speaker: Little Dinosaur
transcript.text: Yeah?

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: Hey, did you know it hurts when you stick one of these in your eye?

transcript.speaker: Little Dinosaur
transcript.text: Hee hee! Good one, Mom; I almost believed you!!

setting: Prehistoric landscape with a rocky outcrop
situation: A mother dinosaur tells her child that little dinosaurs must listen to their mothers, but the child keeps asking why. When the mother claims experience helps avoid danger, a green dinosaur offers a painful-sounding fact about sticking a sharp object in your eye. The child laughs it off, thinking the mother is joking.
punchline: The child is so used to dismissing his mother's authority that even a genuine warning about real danger is taken as a joke.
summary: A parent's demand for obedience falls flat when the kid treats her sincere safety warning as a punchline.

title: Dogbert Borrows Dilbert's Truck-Destroying Gadget

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: May I play with your "Sonic Obliterator" invention?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sure.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just be careful. It has a hair trigger and can blow a truck to bits.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Neat!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You have to show them that you trust them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll be down at the post office truck yard.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dogbert asks to play with Dilbert's "Sonic Obliterator" invention, and Dilbert hands it over with a casual warning that it has a hair trigger and can destroy a truck. Dilbert smugly remarks that you have to show people you trust them, while Dogbert announces he is heading to the post office truck yard with the weapon.
punchline: Dogbert intends to use the truck-destroying weapon on post office trucks, turning Dilbert's careless trust into a recipe for destruction.
summary: After being handed a dangerous gadget with a friendly warning, Dogbert cheerfully heads off to test it on a lot full of mail trucks.

title: Jury Sentences Attorney for Obnoxiousness

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: Has the jury reached a verdict?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, Your Honor. We find the defense attorney poorly dressed and obnoxious. We sentence him to death.

transcript.speaker: Judge
transcript.text: I don't think you can do that.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Furthermore, we find that Your Honor looks fetching in a black muumuu.

setting: A courtroom
situation: A judge asks the jury whether it has reached a verdict. The jury foreman, Dogbert, announces that the defense attorney is poorly dressed and obnoxious and sentences him to death. When the judge objects that the jury cannot do that, Dogbert responds by adding a comment about the judge's appearance in his black robe.
punchline: The jury ignores the legal objection entirely and answers it with an insult, mocking the judge's robe as a muumuu, showing the jury has no regard for legal limits.
summary: A jury delivers an absurd and unlawful verdict against a lawyer based purely on his looks and personality, then mocks the judge's attire when challenged.

title: Dogbert Names the New Rat

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: If you're going to live here, you need a name.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How about "Mickey"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No... Big trouble. How about "Rodney the Rodent"?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: How about "Bill the Rat"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Vernon the Vermin"?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: "Ratbert"

setting: Dogbert's office, with Dogbert in a chair and the rat on a desk
situation: Dogbert tells a small orange rat that he needs a name if he wants to live there. The rat suggests names, Dogbert rejects the one that is trademark trouble and proposes silly rhyming alliterative names, and the rat finally settles on Ratbert.
punchline: After Dogbert's absurd rhyming name suggestions, the rat gives in and picks the name Ratbert, which fits the same silly pattern.
summary: A talking dog and a stray rodent haggle over naming the rodent, ending with the origin of a familiar character's name.

title: Dinosaur Comeback Tour Plans Copied

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: We'll kick off the dinosaur comeback tour by singing "My Way."

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: Then we'll break the instruments, wade into the crowd and bite the head off somebody in the front row!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Ozzy Osbourne" already did that.

setting: Outdoors on a plain tan background, where Dogbert sits with two dinosaurs
situation: A green dinosaur reads from a sheet of paper, laying out the plan for a dinosaur rock-band comeback tour, beginning with a song and ending with smashing instruments and biting off an audience member's head. Dogbert, sitting between the dinosaurs, points out that the plan has already been carried out by someone else. A gray dinosaur looks on silently.
punchline: The dinosaurs' supposedly fresh and outrageous comeback act is just a copy of Ozzy Osbourne's infamous stage antics, so they are not original and not even prehistoric.
summary: A pair of washed-up dinosaurs plot a shocking rock reunion, only to be told that a famous metal singer has already done every bit of it.

title: Dilbert's Ego Buys a Toupee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Ego
transcript.text: I'm Dilbert's ego. I'd like to update my image with a toupee.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I recommend the "Roy Orbison" model. It comes with sunglasses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Ego
transcript.text: Now I won't have to rely so heavily on my personality.

setting: A toupee shop with wigs displayed on mannequin heads on shelves
situation: A small, fuzzy creature representing Dilbert's ego walks into a wig store and asks to update its image with a toupee. The salesman recommends a Roy Orbison style wig that comes with dark sunglasses. The ego happily puts it on and walks away.
punchline: The ego admits that it needs a flashy new look because its personality alone isn't enough to impress anyone.
summary: A personified ego shops for a rock-star wig and shades to compensate for a lack of charisma.

title: Therapist Diagnoses Hardware Store Obsession

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...And I've had this irrational love for hardware stores as long as I can remember.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I mean... I love them. I actually love them. You gotta help me, Doc.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: I've heard of this... I think the literature refers to it as "a stupid guy-thing."

setting: Therapist's office
situation: Dilbert reclines in a chair during a therapy session and confesses an irrational, intense love for hardware stores, begging the doctor for help. The female therapist, taking notes, responds that it is a known phenomenon.
punchline: The therapist dismisses his supposedly serious psychological problem as a mere 'stupid guy-thing', deflating his earnest plea for help with a gender-stereotype joke.
summary: A man pleads with his therapist to cure his deep affection for hardware stores, only to be told it's a common male quirk.

title: Computers Hypnotize You Into Buying More

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Let me show you around the inside of your computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Neat!

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Here's where we generate the hypnotic signals for your display screen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: To make you think you need more computers.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Good Lord, you've learned to reproduce!

setting: Inside a computer's internal machinery
situation: Ratbert, dressed in a small red superhero costume, gives Dilbert a tour of the inside of his computer. He reveals the machinery that generates hypnotic signals through the display screen. The purpose is to make Dilbert believe he needs more computers.
punchline: Computers manipulate their users into buying more computers, which Dilbert recognizes as the machines having learned to reproduce themselves.
summary: A tiny guide shows a man the hidden hypnotic gear in his computer that tricks him into craving more machines, which he realizes is a form of reproduction.

title: Secretary's Sombrero Phone Calls

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Dilbert, I'm putting you in charge of the department secretary.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: See if you can get him to cut down on the personal phone calls.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... Just be a little more discreet... For example, try not wearing the traditional costume of the countries you're calling.

setting: Office, at the department secretary's desk
situation: The Boss puts Dilbert in charge of supervising the department secretary and asks him to reduce the secretary's personal phone calls. Dilbert confronts the secretary, who is sitting at his desk on the phone wearing a giant sombrero and a colorful poncho-style outfit. Dilbert suggests only that he be more discreet about it.
punchline: Dilbert's mild request to be 'more discreet' implies that the secretary's flamboyant ethnic costume, worn to match the country he is phoning, is the only real problem with his personal calls.
summary: A manager hands Dilbert the task of curbing a secretary's private calls, but the secretary turns out to be dressing up in the national costume of whoever he is dialing.

title: Dilbert Imagines Robber Stealing Job

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert the Vigilante

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When I get home from work, we'll track down the man who robbed our house and make him pay!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No! It's the robber at my desk. He's stealing my job too!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's an impostor. Look at his hair!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We thought you'd been in a street fight with Vidal Sassoon...

setting: Dilbert's home and his office
situation: Dilbert vows to track down the man who burgled his house and make him pay. At the office he imagines the robber sitting at his desk and stealing his job too, then tells his boss that the real Dilbert is an impostor. The boss replies that they thought Dilbert's wild hair meant he'd been in a street fight.
punchline: Dilbert's paranoid accusation falls flat because the boss notes the look-alike has a punk mohawk, joking that the impostor's hairstyle looks like the result of a street fight with Vidal Sassoon.
summary: A burgled and paranoid Dilbert pictures the thief taking over his workstation, only to have his boss mock the intruder's spiky haircut.

title: Dinosaurs Admire Time-Saving Computer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You dinosaurs have probably never seen a computer.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This makes me so efficient I can save hours every day.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: What do you do with all the spare time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I work on the computer.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Wow! Then you can save even more time!

setting: Dilbert's desk at the office, with dinosaurs looking on
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and condescendingly tells two dinosaurs they have probably never seen one. He brags that it saves him hours every day, and a dinosaur asks what he does with the spare time. Dilbert admits he spends it working on the computer, and the dinosaur happily concludes he can save even more time.
punchline: Dilbert's time saved by the computer is spent entirely on using the computer, so the supposed efficiency gains are circular and never actually free up any time.
summary: A boastful programmer learns from some prehistoric visitors that his labor-saving machine mostly just consumes the hours it claims to save.

title: Dilbert's Pity Date Goes Wrong

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heather, there's something I must tell you.

transcript.speaker: Heather
transcript.text: Stop... stop right there. I know what you're going to say.

transcript.speaker: Heather
transcript.text: Although it's our first date, you find yourself very attracted to me.

transcript.speaker: Heather
transcript.text: You are stunned by my grace and beauty, and you hope we can be more than friends.

transcript.speaker: Heather
transcript.text: Let me set you straight, Dilbert: This is a a pity date. My standards are too high for you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, I just wanted to tell you that your dress was tucked into the back of your pantyhose all night.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How was your date?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Man, it doesn't get any better than that!

setting: A restaurant table on a first date, then Dilbert's home
situation: On a first date, Dilbert tries to tell Heather something, but she interrupts and presumes he is smitten with her. She declares it a pity date and says her standards are too high for him. Dilbert reveals he only wanted to tell her that her dress had been tucked into her pantyhose all night, and later tells Dogbert it was a great date.
punchline: Heather's arrogant assumption is deflated by the embarrassing truth, and Dilbert's delighted reaction implies he got revenge, or that this was the best his dates ever go.
summary: A conceited date presumes her companion is smitten, only to learn he was merely trying to warn her about a wardrobe malfunction.

title: Dilbert Smokes the Exploding Cigar

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert, look what I got at the joke store: exploding cigars!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Heh-heh... these are hilarious - watch.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: KAPOW!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think you're supposed to get other people to smoke them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Too late now; I'm hooked.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a box of exploding cigars he bought at a joke store. He lights one to demonstrate how funny it is and it blows up in his face, leaving him sprawled on the floor. Dogbert points out that the prank is meant to be played on other people.
punchline: Dilbert pranks himself by smoking the trick cigar, and when Dogbert points out the mistake he deadpans that it's too late because he's now hooked, a smoking pun delivered while lying injured.
summary: A man buys a novelty cigar to amuse his dog and ends up flattened by the blast he meant to inflict on someone else.

title: Bumped Passenger Duct-Taped to Wing

transcript.speaker: Airline Agent
transcript.text: I'm sorry, sir, but you've been "bumped."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got a ticket! I demand satisfaction! I'll call the president of your stupid company!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if there's really such a thing as the "duct tape section."

setting: Airline check-in counter, then the outside of an airplane
situation: Dilbert is told at the Happy Airline counter that he has been bumped from his flight. He angrily insists he has a ticket and threatens to call the airline's president. In the final panel he is duct-taped to the outside of the airplane, wondering if the airline really has a duct tape section.
punchline: The airline's idea of handling an angry bumped passenger is to literally tape him to the plane's exterior, turning the euphemism of seating sections into a grim reality.
summary: A furious traveler who complains about being denied his seat ends up bound to the outside of the plane as an unwilling, very literal passenger.

title: Dinosaur Masseur Hurts Spa Clients

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, I'd like you to be the masseur for my new age miracle spa.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Dinosaurs don't know much about massage.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That's okay. Just hurt the clients as much as possible.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Won't they get angry?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Bob, Bob, Bob... you really aren't tuned to the new age, are you?

setting: Dogbert's office, at a conference table
situation: Dogbert offers Bob the dinosaur a job as the masseur at his new age miracle spa. Bob admits he knows little about massage, and Dogbert says that doesn't matter as long as he hurts the clients as much as possible. Bob worries the clients will get angry, and Dogbert patronisingly says Bob doesn't understand the new age.
punchline: Dogbert implies that new age spa customers will happily pay for painful treatment and believe it is doing them good, so cruelty is a feature rather than a flaw.
summary: A scheming dog hires a clueless dinosaur to run a trendy spa's massages, certain that customers will accept any amount of pain as spiritual healing.

title: Dogbert Cries Over Lost Inheritance

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I haven't been able to cry over Dilbert's death.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I really miss him, but I keep my sorrow bottled inside.

transcript.speaker: Therapist
transcript.text: Did you know that dogs can't legally inherit from humans?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Waaah!!

setting: Therapist's office
situation: Dogbert lies on a therapist's couch and says he hasn't been able to cry over Dilbert's death, claiming he keeps his sorrow bottled up. The therapist offers a trick to bring out his tears by pointing out that dogs can't legally inherit from humans. Dogbert immediately bursts into loud wailing.
punchline: Dogbert's real grief is not for Dilbert but for the inheritance he can't collect, and the therapist's remark exposes his mercenary motives.
summary: A pet's therapy session reveals that the only thing that can make him weep over his owner's death is the loss of an inheritance.

title: Secretary Crushes Paper Clip Insecurity

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's the new secretary for the department working out?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think he's having a self-image problem.

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Sure, I'm a secretary, but watch me crush this paper clip!!

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: RRRR

setting: Office, near the break area and the secretary's desk
situation: A bald coworker holding a coffee cup asks Dilbert how the department's new male secretary is doing. Dilbert says the man seems to have a self-image problem. In the last panel the secretary, grinning at his desk, flexes his hand to crush a paper clip while insisting he is a secretary.
punchline: The secretary overcompensates for his job's lack of macho status by showing off his strength on a paper clip, proving Dilbert's point about his insecurity.
summary: A new male secretary tries to prove his toughness by squeezing a tiny office supply, confirming a colleague's remark about his shaky self-image.

title: Dogbert Gives Terrible Hospital Directions

transcript.speaker: Driver
transcript.text: Hey dog! What's the quickest way to go to the hospital?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Drive as fast as you can into that tree.

transcript.speaker: Driver
transcript.text: What's the second quickest way?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hmm... Well, go left, then right, right, left, left, left, right, left, left, left, left.

transcript.speaker: Driver
transcript.text: Thanks!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Actually, I have no idea how to get to the hospital...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: But I didn't want him to think I'm a jerk.

setting: A country road with grass fields
situation: A driver stops and asks Dogbert for the quickest route to the hospital. Dogbert sarcastically tells him to crash into a tree, then gives a long string of random left and right turns. As the driver leaves, Dogbert admits he has no idea where the hospital is.
punchline: Dogbert gives deliberately useless directions and then claims he did it so the driver wouldn't think he's a jerk, even though he already suggested a fatal crash.
summary: A motorist asking a dog for help gets a deadly suggestion followed by a made-up string of turns, all to avoid seeming rude.

title: Lazy Brain Appreciates Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's one of those days my brain feels lazy.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd better avoid any mental stimulation.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's times like this I really appreciate knowing you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dogbert wanders around humming, thinking to himself that his brain feels lazy and he should avoid anything mentally stimulating. He then sits on Dilbert's lap, telling him he appreciates knowing him at times like this. Dilbert, sitting in his armchair, thanks him.
punchline: Dogbert's compliment is actually an insult: Dilbert is so dull that spending time with him provides no mental stimulation, and Dilbert fails to notice and politely thanks him.
summary: A sluggish-minded dog picks the most boring companion he knows to relax with, and the oblivious man takes it as praise.

title: Cloning Dilbert Goes Horribly Wrong

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert and the Garbage Man try to clone Dilbert back to life.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Phzup!

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: Aaagh! Run for your life!!! It's a hideous, disgusting creature!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would you care for a little "Arm and Hammer"?

setting: A makeshift cloning lab with a zapping machine, and an alley with a garbage can
situation: Dogbert and the Garbage Man use a sparking machine to clone Dilbert back to life. The Garbage Man, with his hair standing on end, sees the result and screams in horror, running away and losing his hat. Dilbert emerges in a garbage can, and Dogbert offers him a box of Arm and Hammer baking soda.
punchline: The clone is so hideous that it horrifies even the Garbage Man, and Dogbert's offer of baking soda implies that the revived Dilbert smells bad, like a refrigerator or garbage in need of deodorizing.
summary: A resurrection experiment succeeds, but the reborn engineer is so repulsive that the helper flees while the dog offers him a deodorizer.

title: Walnut-Sized Brains Explain Cult Membership

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: How did we ever allow ourselves to be drawn into Dogbert's evil cult?

transcript.speaker: Dawn
transcript.text: Maybe he has strange hypnotic powers. Maybe we were mesmerized by his oratorical skill.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It says here you have brains the size of a walnut.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: What's your point?

setting: Undefined pale green background, apparently an interview or questioning scene
situation: Two dinosaur-like creatures, one green and spiny and one gray with long horns and a tongue sticking out, wonder how they ended up in Dogbert's evil cult. One suggests Dogbert has hypnotic powers or amazing oratory. Dilbert, holding a notepad, points out that their brains are only the size of a walnut.
punchline: The creatures are looking for mystical explanations for their gullibility, but their tiny brains obviously explain it, and they are too dim to even grasp the insult.
summary: Two befuddled dinosaurs puzzle over how they were recruited into a cult, never realizing their pea-sized intellects are the obvious answer.

title: Dilbert's Holographic Chili Recipe

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yikes! Dilbert's invention is alive!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (hologram)
transcript.text: I am a holographic recording of the late Dilbert, with a message to Dogbert from beyond the grave.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (hologram)
transcript.text: ...and my recipe for chile con carne is as follows...

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of his holographic projector
situation: Dogbert is startled when a projector invented by Dilbert flashes to life. A hologram of the deceased Dilbert announces it is a recorded message for Dogbert from beyond the grave. Dogbert then settles in with a notepad as the hologram begins reciting a chile con carne recipe.
punchline: The dramatic message from beyond the grave turns out to be nothing more than a cooking recipe, an anticlimax.
summary: A ghostly projected recording of a dead inventor turns out to be delivering a dinner recipe instead of a solemn farewell.

title: Elbonia's Mud-Only Economy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The basic problem with your economy is that the only product you make is mud...

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: So?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nobody needs mud. Who the heck is in charge of planning this economy, anyway?

setting: Muddy landscape in Elbonia, with a mud hut in the background
situation: Dilbert visits Elbonia and lectures a group of tall-hatted locals about their economy, pointing out that their only product is mud. He asks who is responsible for planning it. In the last panel the Elbonians stand silently while a smiling pink pig sits nearby, implying the pig is in charge.
punchline: The pig sitting grinning in the final panel is the implied central planner, suggesting that only a pig would design an economy built entirely on worthless mud.
summary: An outsider mocks a country whose sole export is worthless mud, only to discover that a pig is apparently running things.

title: Timid Dilbert Builds Blanket Fort

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm feeling timid today...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I felt timid yesterday too...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Holy cheese! I may be a timid person.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've decided to build a blanket fort with the living room furniture and live in it forever.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm so proud of you.

setting: Dilbert's home, living room
situation: Dilbert sits and thinks to himself that he feels timid today and also felt timid yesterday. He realizes he may be a timid person, then decides to respond by building a blanket fort out of the living room furniture and living in it forever. Dogbert sarcastically tells him he is proud of him.
punchline: Dilbert's solution to discovering he is timid is to hide away permanently in a blanket fort, and Dogbert's deadpan pride mocks this extreme retreat as if it were an achievement.
summary: After realizing he is a shy person, Dilbert resolves to hide forever in a fort made of blankets and furniture while Dogbert cheers him on.

title: Sonic Obliterator Has Limited Household Use

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This could be my most important technical achievement yet. I'll call it the "Sonic Obliterator."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hmm... catchy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This baby can blast a buffalo into random particles in about half a nanosecond.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Of course, it might have limited application around the house.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At least the buffaloes will show us some respect.

setting: Dilbert's home workbench
situation: Dilbert proudly shows off a gadget he has built, naming it the Sonic Obliterator and boasting that it can vaporize a buffalo almost instantly. He then admits it probably isn't very useful around the house. Dogbert replies that at least buffaloes will respect them.
punchline: Dogbert's deadpan reply treats the absurdly powerful but impractical weapon as a way to command respect from buffaloes, the only thing it is actually good for.
summary: An engineer unveils a ridiculously powerful weapon, concedes it has no domestic use, and his dog points out its one perk.

title: Dilbert Hires a Burglar Cleaner

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert hires a cleaning person

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And your name is..?

transcript.speaker: Cleaning Person
transcript.text: Call me Mr. Tidy.

transcript.text: The agency says you're experienced.

transcript.text: Yeah, I've cleaned out some of the nicer homes in this area.

transcript.speaker: Cleaning Person

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert interviews a punk-looking cleaning person with an eyepatch and mohawk who calls himself Mr. Tidy. The man brags about having 'cleaned out' nicer homes in the area, then suggests Dilbert load all his possessions into his van so he can clean them at his own place. Dilbert naively asks only whether that costs extra.
punchline: The cleaner is obviously a thief using 'cleaned out' as a double meaning, and Dilbert is so oblivious that he worries about the price instead of being robbed.
summary: A shady-looking housecleaner hints at his burglary past and talks his clueless client into handing over all his belongings.

title: Swapping Jobs With Your Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is a very interesting employee suggestion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Thank you, sir.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If I read this correctly...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You observed that everybody is smarter than his boss...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Exactly...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So we all just switch jobs with our bosses and boost productivity by 200%!!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've decided to do a limited trial...

transcript.speaker: Janitor
transcript.text: Something died in the stairwell. Take care of it.

setting: The Boss's office
situation: Dilbert submits an employee suggestion that everybody is smarter than their boss, so workers and bosses should swap jobs to double productivity. The Boss reads it and says he will run a limited trial. He applies it by having Dilbert swap with the janitor, who orders Dilbert to deal with a dead animal in the stairwell.
punchline: The Boss takes the suggestion about swapping jobs with bosses and applies it in the most insulting way, demoting Dilbert to janitor duty instead of trading places with him.
summary: A well-meant efficiency idea backfires when management implements it as a punishment rather than a promotion.

title: Bank Thinks Dilbert Is Dead

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My credit card has been canceled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The stupid bank's computer thinks I died.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is an opportunity for some righteous indignation. I love that.

transcript.speaker: Credit Card Employee
transcript.text: Hello, credit card department, an underpaid employee speaking.

transcript.speaker: Credit Card Employee
transcript.text: Well, yes, apparently you are alive. But it would be very difficult to reprogram the computer...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sure you'll find a solution.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Kill him?

transcript.speaker: Credit Card Employee
transcript.text: Unless you'd rather read this computer manual.

setting: Dilbert's home and a bank's credit card department office
situation: Dilbert's credit card has been canceled because the bank's computer wrongly believes he is dead. He phones the credit card department to complain, and the employee admits he is clearly alive but says reprogramming the computer would be too difficult. When Dilbert insists a solution must exist, the employee's coworker suggests killing him, and the employee offers reading the computer manual as the alternative.
punchline: Rather than fix the bank's database error, the employee considers it easier to make the data true by killing Dilbert, with reading the manual as the only other option.
summary: A man declared dead by a bank's computer finds that the easiest fix on offer is to make the record accurate.

title: Blind Date With Man-Eating Janet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: I will never go on another blind date.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, Jabba... er... I mean, Janet, have you dated many other men?

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Yes, but they all disappeared without a trace.

transcript.speaker: Janet
transcript.text: Incidentally, you look delicious tonight.

setting: A restaurant table, evening
situation: Dilbert sits at a restaurant table on a blind date with a very large woman and privately vows never to do this again. He accidentally calls her 'Jabba' before correcting himself and asks about her dating history. In silhouette, she answers that her previous dates all vanished without a trace and says he looks delicious.
punchline: Janet's previous dates disappeared without a trace and she calls Dilbert 'delicious', implying she literally eats the men she dates, much like Jabba the Hutt.
summary: A man on a miserable blind date learns that his enormous companion's former suitors have all mysteriously vanished, and she seems to be eyeing him as her next meal.

title: Engineer's Pills Keep Dilbert Out Of The Way

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd fix it myself but I know it takes special tools...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Plus I would just have to order a part... and I'm pretty busy...

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: Take two of these...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Engineer's pills"?

transcript.speaker: Ed
transcript.text: They'll knock you out until I'm gone.

setting: Dilbert's home living room, next to a broken old television
situation: A TV repairman from Ed's TV Repair arrives to fix Dilbert's television. Dilbert, an engineer, hovers and makes excuses about why he could have fixed it himself, rambling about special tools and ordering parts. The repairman hands him pills labeled "engineer's pills" that will knock him out until the repairman has finished and left.
punchline: The repairman is so used to engineers meddling and second-guessing his work that he keeps a sedative on hand to knock them out and keep them out of his way.
summary: A television repairman has a sneaky remedy for customers who can't stop hovering and explaining how they'd do the job themselves.

title: Dogbert Ambushes Guilty Businessman Randomly

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to become an ambush reporter, like Mike Wallace.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is it true you made all of your money unethically and you're having an affair?

transcript.speaker: Businessman
transcript.text: Yes!! Yes!! How did you find me?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You were chosen randomly.

setting: Dilbert's living room, then outside with a stranger
situation: Dogbert, sitting by Dilbert as he reads a newspaper, announces he is becoming an ambush reporter. He confronts a businessman with a briefcase, accusing him of making his money unethically and having an affair. The man immediately confesses and asks how Dogbert found him, and Dogbert says it was random.
punchline: The businessman's instant confession of both wrongdoings reveals he is guilty of everything, and that Dogbert's random accusation hit the mark, implying any random businessperson would be guilty.
summary: A dog playing investigative journalist picks a random suit-wearing stranger, accuses him of scandal, and gets a panicked admission of guilt.

title: Not Enough Quality Women, Sadly

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: About 400 women turned me down for dates this year.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can only conclude one thing . . .

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not enough quality women?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sadly.

setting: Grassy hilltop outdoors
situation: Dilbert sits on a hill with Dogbert and says about 400 women rejected him for dates this year. He says he can only draw one conclusion, and Dogbert guesses it is that there aren't enough quality women. Dilbert sadly agrees, blaming the women rather than himself.
punchline: Dilbert blames the supply of 'quality women' for hundreds of rejections instead of considering that the problem might be him.
summary: After being rejected by hundreds of women in a year, a lonely engineer decides the real issue must be a shortage of worthy dates.

title: Describing Feelings: Wheat Field, Then Tractor

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: It's hard to express how I feel when I'm with you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Try.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Imagine a field of golden wheat on a sunny spring day. Birds are singing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There... that wasn't too hard.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: Now imagine a tractor on your chest...

setting: A restaurant table during a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits across from a woman at a restaurant table. She says she can't express her feelings about him, so he tells her to try, and she describes a pleasant image of a golden wheat field with singing birds. When he says that was easy, she reveals the other half of the image: a tractor crushing his chest.
punchline: The woman's warm, romantic imagery turns out to be a setup for a crushing, suffocating comparison, revealing that being with Dilbert feels oppressive to her.
summary: A date starts out with a dreamy pastoral image and then flattens the poor guy with a heavy farm-machinery metaphor.

title: Tearjerker Engineering Newsletter About Lost Data

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got to make the engineering newsletter more interesting.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It needs pathos and human drama.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "How to cope with the loss of loved data..."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait... I better get some tissues.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert is tasked with making the engineering newsletter more interesting and decides it needs pathos and human drama. He then reads aloud a draft article titled 'How to cope with the loss of loved data...' from a long printout. Dogbert, listening nearby, reacts as if it were truly moving and goes to fetch tissues.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of human drama is an emotional article about grieving for lost computer data, and Dogbert's tearful reaction shows how absurdly well it works on the geek audience.
summary: An engineer spices up a dull company newsletter with a melodramatic piece about mourning deleted files, and his dog is moved to tears.

title: Blind Date With Giant-Headed Librarian

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've got a blind date with the lady who works at the library reference desk.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What if she's ugly?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks aren't important. She sounded very smart over the phone, and I'm attracted to intelligent women.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh... right.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... should I talk, or will you be reading my thoughts directly?

setting: Dilbert's bedroom, then a restaurant table
situation: Dilbert gets ready for a blind date with a library reference desk worker while Dogbert, lying on the bed, asks what if she's ugly. Dilbert insists he only cares about intelligence. At dinner his date turns out to have an enormous, egg-shaped head, and Dilbert nervously wonders if she can read his mind.
punchline: Dilbert's claim that looks don't matter is undercut when his date's huge head makes him assume she is so intelligent she can read thoughts, showing he still judges by appearance.
summary: A man who swears he only wants a smart partner meets a date whose oversized head makes him fear she's psychic.

title: Dilbert's Disastrous Pickup Line

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've noticed that all the cool guys use gentle kidding with women.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Women must like it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Excuse me, Miss, does your face hurt? It's killing me!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Giggle Giggle snort

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The cool guys must hate it when this happens to them.

setting: A city street beside a brick wall
situation: Dilbert reasons that because cool guys tease women gently, women must enjoy it. He tries an insulting pickup line on a woman, who apparently reacts with a giggle and a snort, and he ends up upside down in a garbage can with his legs sticking out, musing that cool guys must hate this outcome.
punchline: Dilbert's flawed logic and clumsy insult get him thrown into the trash, while he wryly assumes this never happens to the genuinely cool guys he's imitating.
summary: After copying what he thinks smooth men do, Dilbert delivers a rude chat-up line and gets stuffed headfirst into a trash can.

title: Deprogramming Dogbert's Cult With Ridiculousness

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have a plan to deprogram you from the control of Dogbert's cult.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My theory is that the brain reflexively embraces the most ridiculous explanation of reality.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, we just have to think of something more ridiculous than following a dog's commands.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Like listening to you?

setting: Office or open area, plain peach background
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert's cult followers, including Ratbert, that he has a plan to deprogram them. He explains his theory that the brain clings to the most ridiculous explanation of reality, so he only needs to find something sillier than obeying a dog. Ratbert responds by suggesting that listening to Dilbert is exactly that.
punchline: Ratbert sarcastically points out that listening to Dilbert's absurd deprogramming theory is more ridiculous than following a dog, undermining his entire plan.
summary: A man hoping to free cult members from a talking dog's influence gets mocked when one follower names him as the more absurd authority.

title: Elbonians Suspect Capitalism Is Mud Espionage

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: How do we know you came to Elbonia just to teach us capitalism?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Yeah... maybe you came to steal our secret process for making mud!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dirt and water?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: He knows...

transcript.speaker: Pig
transcript.text: We'll have to kill him.

setting: A barren, muddy landscape in Elbonia
situation: Dilbert is in Elbonia to teach the locals about capitalism. The suspicious tall-hatted Elbonians accuse him of really coming to steal their secret mud-making process. When Dilbert correctly guesses that it is just dirt and water, they decide he knows too much and must be killed.
punchline: The Elbonians' supposedly closely guarded trade secret is trivially obvious (dirt and water), and they treat Dilbert's casual guess as grounds for murder.
summary: Paranoid villagers fear an outsider wants their mud recipe, then resolve to eliminate him when he effortlessly names the two ingredients.

title: Old Woman Eaten By Handbag

transcript.text: Wild coyotes in the handbag... I've seen this before.

transcript.speaker: Handbag
transcript.text: Woof! Urp

setting: Grocery store express checkout lane
situation: An elderly woman with a cart far over the ten-item limit holds up the express lane, pulling rank on the cashier because of her age and claiming her coupons and an odd check are lost in her handbag. When she rummages deep into the bag, she is swallowed up and only her legs remain visible, to the cashier's horror. The handbag then burps, and the cashier calmly notes he has seen it before while Dilbert looks on.
punchline: The entitled shopper who makes everyone wait while she rummages gets literally devoured by her own handbag, and the cashier's weary familiarity implies it happens regularly.
summary: A pushy senior citizen who abuses the express lane is consumed by her bottomless purse as the unfazed clerk recalls similar incidents.

title: Dogbert Frees His Dancing Dinosaurs

transcript.speaker: Dinosaurs
transcript.text: We're free! We're free!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boy... you don't know ugly 'til you've seen dinosaurs dance.

setting: Dogbert's home, on his pedestal, with two dinosaur followers beside him
situation: Dogbert announces that he is dissolving his cult and releasing his two dinosaur followers to do whatever they like. The delighted dinosaurs leap and dance around celebrating their freedom. Dogbert watches them and comments on how awful the dancing looks.
punchline: Dogbert generously grants his followers freedom, only to regret it immediately because the dinosaurs' celebratory dancing is hideous to watch.
summary: After setting his two dinosaur disciples loose, Dogbert is treated to an exuberant victory dance he finds painful to witness.

title: Dilbert's Mysterious Gadget Inheritance

transcript.text: I'm just the custodian.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Can I change my guess?

setting: A tabletop or counter in a plain room with a purple-gray wall
situation: A green dinosaur asks Dogbert about the odd gadget Dilbert left him in his will. Dogbert says he is just the custodian, and the dinosaur offers an elaborate technobabble guess for what the device might be. Dogbert's own guess is a bathroom soap dispenser, which the gadget plainly resembles.
punchline: The dinosaur's grand technical theory is deflated when Dogbert correctly identifies the gadget as a mundane soap dispenser, leaving the dinosaur embarrassed and wanting to retract his guess.
summary: A pompous guess about a mystery device crumbles when it turns out to be an ordinary item found in a restroom.

title: Dogbert's Statistical Case for Salting First

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You shouldn't salt your food before tasting it.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a calculated risk...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The average mouthful of food is five percent of the total serving.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So timid salters eat five percent of almost every meal with too little salt...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Because only one time in a thousand is food too salty to begin with.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Therefore, over a lifetime you experience almost five percent less salt-related happiness than I do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not necessarily. I usually salt my tongue after the first swallow.

setting: A dinner table at a restaurant or home
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit at a table with plates of food. Dilbert tells Dogbert not to salt his food before tasting it, and Dogbert responds with a pseudo-scientific statistical argument about the odds of food being too salty and the lifetime happiness lost by timid salters. Dilbert ends the exchange with a deadpan retort about salting his tongue instead.
punchline: Dilbert undercuts Dogbert's elaborate probability argument by revealing he simply salts his tongue after the first swallow, avoiding the risk entirely and losing no salt-related happiness.
summary: A dog uses faulty-but-impressive math to justify seasoning a meal in advance, only to be topped by his companion's absurdly simple workaround.

setting: A laboratory room with a door marked LAB
situation: A miserable lab rat sits on a ledge, thinking about how much he hates his life and the endless macaroni and cheese he is fed. He suspects the diet may be a deliberate way of killing him, then plans a prison-style escape by going 'over the wall'. He corrects himself, realizing that as a rat he can simply go through the wall.
punchline: The rat borrows the prison-break cliche of going 'over the wall' before realizing that being a rat, he can just go through it.
summary: A fed-up laboratory rat plots a dramatic escape and then catches the obvious rodent shortcut.

title: Scared Dogbert Needs Veterinary Care

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

punchline: The vet describes Dogbert's condition as if he were a car getting a suspension upgrade, implying the scare left him with a physical change, in a darkly absurd 'silver lining' about handling better on corners.
summary: A prank on a peaceful pet leads to a vet visit where the doctor offers a bizarrely car-like silver lining.

situation: Dilbert's date asks to hold hands, and he demurs because his dog, who is prudish, is somewhere in the house. She laughs at him, insulting both the dog and Dilbert as a wimp for letting a pet rule his house. Dilbert laughs and gives his blessing as Dogbert, holding a spray device, stands ready beside the couch.
punchline: Dilbert was telling the truth that Dogbert is really the master, so he gleefully lets his date insult the dog and then watches Dogbert get his revenge.
summary: A woman mocks a man for being bossed around by his pet, not realizing the pet really is in charge and is about to retaliate.

summary: A friendly dinosaur punishes irritating braggarts, spoilers and salesmen by tearing off their underwear, and the final panel suggests a patronizing tech expert is next.

title: Dogbert's Credit Card World Domination

situation: Dogbert returns from the mailbox gleefully holding a newly approved Macys credit card and explains his plan to conquer the world. He intends to build credit history, collect cards from every bank, and take cash advances to fund a giant global lottery. Dilbert, working on a sock puppet, listens and then remarks that most dogs would settle for a chew toy.
punchline: Dogbert's world-domination scheme is just an elaborate credit card and lottery gimmick, and Dilbert deflates it by noting that ordinary dogs have far more modest ambitions.
summary: A scheming dog plots to rule the planet by stacking up credit cards and bribing humanity with lottery tickets, while his owner wryly wishes he wanted something simpler.

title: Dogbert Plans Crimes, Dilbert Takes Blame

punchline: Dogbert casually plans to commit crimes and frame his owner for them, and treats Dilbert's obvious objection to taking the blame as mere selfishness.
summary: A scheming dog informs his owner that he intends to break the law with impunity since the human will bear all the liability.

situation: Dilbert shows Dogbert a photo album and introduces his late Uncle Phil, who died hang gliding. Dogbert asks if he hit a tree, and Dilbert says he didn't read the manual carefully. In the last panel Uncle Phil stands on a hang glider, hanging from a noose from a tree, wondering if there is another reason it's called hang gliding.
punchline: Uncle Phil misunderstood 'hang gliding' as literally hanging himself from a tree, a fatal result of not reading the manual.
summary: A family photo album reveals an uncle whose misunderstanding of a sport's name led to a grim and absurd end.

situation: Dogbert meets Dilbert's ego, which looks like a piece of broccoli, and offers it a toupee since it is insecure about being bald. Dogbert bluntly points out that it will look like broccoli either way, and the ego settles for avoiding the worse fate of bald broccoli.
punchline: Dilbert's ego is so fragile and self-absorbed that, even after being told it resembles broccoli, its only concern is not being bald.
summary: A dog offers a hairpiece to a self-conscious vegetable-shaped ego and gets a surprisingly low-bar response to his honest critique.

title: Dinosaur Explains Mesozoic Practical Jokes

situation: Dogbert, sitting on a stool, remarks that he always imagined dinosaurs as much bigger than Bob. Bob, a small green dinosaur, explains that practical jokes were popular in the Mesozoic era. A thought bubble shows a dinosaur buying a giant plastic bone and fake vomit at a joke shop, hinting that the dinosaurs' extinction came from the joke-shop items.
punchline: Dinosaurs went extinct because they were lured into tar pits and wiped out by prank-shop items, a silly, absurd explanation for why they disappeared.
summary: A small dinosaur blames the Mesozoic craze for gag shop novelties for the downfall of his supposedly gigantic species.

title: Dogbert's Fake Courtroom Confession

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm the one who killed those people. I did it for love and for money and revenge!!

situation: Dogbert interrupts a trial, shouting that the defendant is innocent. He then stands on his chair and dramatically confesses to the killings, citing love, money and revenge as motives. He then admits it wasn't true and he just wanted to say it.
punchline: Dogbert disrupts a murder trial with a false confession simply to fulfil a personal wish to deliver a dramatic courtroom outburst.
summary: A small dog stops a trial with a theatrical confession to murder, then admits he was only indulging a lifelong urge.

title: Boss Sneezes Into Dilbert's Shirt

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Boss, I need to talk to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel you don't respect me...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an intangible thing...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Sneeze coming...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I see it in your body language...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: AAH...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and sometimes the things you say...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: RRRRIIP

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: CHOOO

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This has been something less than a victory for workers everywhere.

setting: Dilbert's office
situation: Dilbert works up the courage to confront the Boss about feeling disrespected. While Dilbert earnestly explains, the Boss is distracted by an impending sneeze, grabs Dilbert's shirt, rips it off, and sneezes into it. Dilbert is left shirtless and defeated.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to stand up for himself about being disrespected is undercut when the Boss literally uses his shirt as a tissue, proving the disrespect and leaving Dilbert with a wry understatement about his failed protest.
summary: A employee's brave attempt to air his grievance ends with his manager tearing off his shirt to sneeze into it.

title: Dogbert Requests House Painting Before Death

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and the doctor gave me just a year to live.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry, little guy... I don't know how you'll manage without me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Would it be too much trouble to paint the house before you go?

setting: Dilbert's living room, with Dilbert seated in an armchair
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair and tells his dog Dogbert that his doctor has given him only a year to live. He apologizes to Dogbert, worrying about how the dog will cope without him. Dogbert responds not with grief but by asking Dilbert to paint the house before he dies.
punchline: Instead of showing sympathy, Dogbert coldly sees his owner's terminal diagnosis as a chance to get a chore done, revealing how self-interested and unsentimental he is.
summary: A man breaks the news of his terminal illness to his pet, who answers with a selfish household request.

title: Dilbert Explains Capitalism to Elbonians

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The first thing you Elbonians must understand about capitalism is the incentive system.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you're willing to work twelve hours a day, eventually the guy who owns your factory will get rich.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Am I missing something here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you guys get to watch great TV shows based on the millionaire's life!

setting: Muddy Elbonian landscape outdoors
situation: Dilbert lectures a group of Elbonians in tall hats about how capitalism's incentive system works. He explains that if they work twelve hours a day, their factory owner will eventually get rich. One Elbonian asks what's in it for them, and Dilbert says they get to watch TV shows about the millionaire's life.
punchline: The supposed incentive for the workers is not wealth for themselves but the chance to watch entertainment about their boss's wealthy lifestyle, exposing how lopsided the system is.
summary: A cheerful lecture on free-market motivation reveals that the workers' only reward for endless labor is watching dramatizations of their employer's riches.

title: Dogbert's Nose Toupee Infomercial

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Tired of being teased because of thinning nose hair?

transcript.speaker: Television
transcript.text: Get the "Rivco Nose Toupee" for only $9.95!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's totally undetectable.

setting: Dilbert's living room, in front of the television
situation: Dogbert sits on a rug watching a television infomercial that pitches a toupee made for thinning nose hair. The ad shows a small rug-like toupee, and Dilbert, standing nearby, remarks that it is totally undetectable.
punchline: The pitch for an absurdly tiny hairpiece is undercut by the fact that the product is literally a miniature rug, and calling it undetectable is a joke about how silly a nose toupee would be.
summary: A late-night television ad hawks a hairpiece for your nostrils, and the most that can be said for it is that nobody will notice.

title: Dinosaurs Evolved Into Birds For Miles

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I read that dinosaurs evolved into the bird family.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: That's exactly correct, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: But most people don't realize that there was a very difficult period when some dinosaurs started evolving into birds.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Learning to fly was the hardest part."

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "And living in trees was a real nuisance."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boy, that sounds tough.

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: The tragic part is that we did it just for the "bonus miles".

setting: A prehistoric landscape with dinosaurs, volcanoes and cliffs
situation: Dogbert chats with a pair of dinosaurs about the theory that dinosaurs evolved into birds. One dinosaur solemnly recounts the hardships of the transition: crash-landing while learning to fly and awkwardly perching in trees. Dogbert sympathizes, and the dinosaur reveals the whole ordeal was for frequent flyer rewards.
punchline: The dinosaur's grave tale of evolutionary suffering ends with the absurd reveal that the motivation was airline "bonus miles," mocking loyalty programs people endure hardship to chase.
summary: A dinosaur gravely describes the painful journey to becoming a bird, only to admit the whole thing was done to rack up airline reward points.

title: Dogbert Channels Living Comedian's Career

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thank you all for coming to Dogbert's "New Age Mineral Water Spa."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After your chowder bath therapy, I will be channeling the spirit of Jackie Mason in Ballroom "B."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He's not dead.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I'll talk to his career.

setting: A New Age mineral water spa, with guests in towels and robes
situation: Dogbert, standing at a lectern, welcomes towel-clad guests to his New Age spa and announces that after chowder bath therapy he will channel the spirit of Jackie Mason. Dilbert points out that Jackie Mason is not dead. Dogbert adapts on the spot and says he'll talk to the comedian's career instead.
punchline: Caught channeling a person who is still alive, Dogbert shrugs it off by claiming he'll commune with the man's career, which is presumably the part that has died.
summary: A scam spa operator's séance plan is undone by a technicality, so he simply changes the target of his supernatural claims.

title: Dogbert Ponders Wasteful Fishing Process

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People catch worms to go fishing.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: People eat fish that just ate worms.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There is definitely a wasted step here.

setting: Dogbert sitting on a red cushion, lost in thought
situation: Dogbert sits meditatively on a red cushion and thinks aloud in thought bubbles about the process of fishing. He notes that people catch worms in order to catch fish, and then eat the fish that just ate the worms. He concludes that the process contains an unnecessary step.
punchline: Dogbert's cynical logic suggests people should just eat the worms directly, skipping the fish, which absurdly treats fishing as an inefficient process to be optimized.
summary: Dogbert muses that humans go through a pointlessly roundabout chain of worms and fish to get a meal.

title: Dinosaurs Plan Elvis-Style Comeback Tour

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: Dogbert, we can't stand hiding around the house anymore.

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: We dinosaurs ruled this planet once. Now we just hide in people's houses, pretending to be extinct.

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: Dawn, it's time for our comeback tour.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I think some of Elvis' jumpsuits will fit.

setting: Inside a house, near a window with pink curtains
situation: Two dinosaurs living secretly in a house complain that they are tired of hiding. The green dinosaur laments that dinosaurs once ruled the planet and now only pretend to be extinct, then proposes a comeback tour to the gray dinosaur. Dogbert, watching from the floor, suggests that Elvis' jumpsuits would fit them.
punchline: Dogbert treats the dinosaurs' comeback tour as a washed-up rock act and implies they'd look like aging, jumpsuit-wearing Elvis, and the old rumor that Elvis is still alive and in hiding ties in with their own pretend extinction.
summary: Fed up with hiding as supposedly extinct creatures, two dinosaurs plan a comeback tour and Dogbert offers them Elvis-style stage outfits.

title: Dilbert Lands in Elbonian Mud

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert takes a slingshot ride to Elbonia's capital.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There it is...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a good thing this whole country is made of mud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have come to teach you capitalism.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Did you bring blue jeans?

setting: Elbonia, a muddy country, seen from the sky and then ground level
situation: Dilbert is launched by slingshot toward Elbonia's capital and plummets toward a landscape of mud huts. He splunks head-first into the mud, relieved that the whole country is mud. Stuck up to his neck, he tells the locals he has come to teach them capitalism, and one asks if he brought blue jeans.
punchline: Dilbert's lofty mission to bring capitalism is met with the locals' only real interest in the West: blue jeans.
summary: A man flung into a mud-covered foreign land announces his economic mission and gets asked about fashion instead.

title: Email Makes Ignoring Faster

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Has your electronic mail system made you more efficient?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a way.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'm getting ignored at the speed of light.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can send electronic mail to us through the Prodigy system, care of Scott Adams, ID number MWPG03A.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Note: This strip is not affiliated with Prodigy in any way.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, at his computer desk
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert, who is sitting at his computer, whether electronic mail has made him more efficient. Dilbert says only in a way, explaining that he is now ignored much faster. In the last panel Dogbert gives out the strip's email contact details through the Prodigy system, with a disclaimer that the strip is not affiliated with Prodigy.
punchline: Email does not make people respond any better; it just means your messages get ignored instantly rather than slowly.
summary: Instant electronic messaging turns out to have sped up only one thing: how quickly a person's messages are brushed aside.

title: Dilbert Agonizes Over Hotel Tipping

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hate fancy hotels like this...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Am I expected to tip the maid when I leave?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could ask that concierge guy...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I trust a guy with a French-sounding job?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...and do I have to tip HIM?

setting: A fancy hotel room, with a suitcase open on the bed
situation: Dilbert, on a business trip, stands in his hotel room and silently frets about hotel etiquette. He wonders whether he should tip the maid as he leaves, then considers asking the concierge for advice. He worries about trusting someone with a French-sounding job title and whether he would have to tip the concierge too.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to resolve his tipping uncertainty by asking an expert just creates another person he might have to tip.
summary: A nervous traveler chases his own tipping anxiety in circles, since every possible source of advice is itself someone who expects a gratuity.

title: Dogbert Vacuums the Dust Bunny

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: (A giant dust bunny pokes Dogbert, who is sitting on a cushion.)

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Holy hairballs! What are you?!!

transcript.speaker: Dust Bunny
transcript.text: I am the "Dust Bunny," an emerging cultural icon.

transcript.speaker: Dust Bunny
transcript.text: Once a year I come to every home and hide clumps of dust under furniture and major appliances.

transcript.speaker: Dust Bunny
transcript.text: You must honor me by decorating closet doors and singing dust hymns.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What about gifts? Do I get any gifts out of this?

transcript.speaker: Dust Bunny
transcript.text: No. The Dust Bunny symbolizes only love, goodwill and very poor housekeeping.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know, it seems harsh, but you have to nip these things in the bud.

transcript.speaker: Dust Bunny
transcript.text: Okay, gifts!

setting: A home living room
situation: A giant dust bunny appears before Dogbert and announces itself as a new holiday icon that demands to be honored with decorations and hymns. When Dogbert asks about gifts and learns there are none, he gets out a vacuum cleaner and destroys the creature.
punchline: Since the dust bunny's holiday promises no gifts and only bad housekeeping, Dogbert cheerfully vacuums it up, and the closing caption suggests he got his 'gifts' in the form of cleaning.
summary: A holiday mascot made of household dust demands worship but offers no presents, so Dogbert gets rid of it with a vacuum cleaner.

title: Dogbert Blames Innocent Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've got to get out of this bad mood somehow.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll have to find somebody innocent to blame... and make him plead for my forgiveness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Is that some kind of an insult?

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dogbert sits on a cushion thinking about how to shake off his bad mood. He decides to find an innocent person to blame and make them beg for forgiveness. He then walks up to Dilbert, who innocently greets him, and Dogbert immediately accuses him of insulting him.
punchline: Dogbert acts on his plan instantly by twisting Dilbert's harmless greeting into an insult, showing he is deliberately picking on an innocent victim to feel better.
summary: A grumpy Dogbert plots to cheer himself up by scapegoating someone blameless, and Dilbert's friendly hello makes him the perfect target.

title: Expecting an Egg, Hoping for Egg

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: We're going to have an egg!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What are you hoping it will be?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Something round and white, about yea big.

setting: A plain room with an orange wall
situation: Bob the dinosaur and Dawn, a gray long-horned creature, announce to Dogbert that they are going to have an egg. Dogbert asks what they are hoping it will turn out to be. Bob answers by describing an ordinary egg, holding his hands apart to show its size.
punchline: Asked what they hope the egg will hatch into, Bob only describes the egg itself, showing the couple has not thought past the egg and giving a deadpan literal answer.
summary: A pair of excited expectant parents is asked what they want their egg to become, and they simply describe an egg.

title: Dilbert Proves Existence Through Junk Mail

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh! Nice pile of mail today!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Resident... Resident... Resident... Ahh, Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I get mail; therefore I am.

setting: Outside at Dilbert's mailbox, then inside his home
situation: Dilbert pulls a big stack of mail from his mailbox and excitedly sorts through it. Nearly every piece is addressed to 'Resident', until he finds one with his actual name on it. Holding that single letter, he concludes that receiving mail proves he exists.
punchline: Dilbert's lonely life is so devoid of real contact that a single letter with his name on it, amid a pile of generic junk mail, is his only proof of existence, a parody of Descartes' 'I think, therefore I am.'
summary: A solitary man sifts through a heap of impersonal mailings and takes comfort in the one envelope bearing his name as evidence that he is real.

title: Dogbert Mocks Dilbert's Own Chatter

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I really enjoy these quiet times we have.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just delicious silence. No annoying noise. No inane chatter.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Apparently you don't listen to you, either.

setting: Dilbert's living room, in an armchair
situation: Dilbert relaxes in a green armchair with Dogbert on his lap, praising how much he enjoys their quiet times together. He goes on at length about the delicious silence and the absence of annoying noise and inane chatter. Dogbert responds that Dilbert doesn't listen to himself either.
punchline: Dilbert's speech praising silence is itself the very inane chatter he claims to dislike, and Dogbert points out his hypocrisy.
summary: A man gushes about the joys of peaceful quiet while talking nonstop, and his dog drily notes that he fails to heed his own noise.

title: Moose Hunt Programmers With Arrows

transcript.speaker: Moose 1
transcript.text: ...When he saw my headlights, he froze and his eyes got big like this.

transcript.speaker: Moose 1
transcript.text: I tracked him back to his computer and waited until he slipped into a programmer's daze...

transcript.speaker: Moose 1
transcript.text: Then I plugged him with an arrow.

transcript.speaker: Moose 2
transcript.text: Wow! You did that without opposable thumbs?!!

setting: A forest, with moose gathered near a tree
situation: A moose boasts to other moose about hunting a human programmer, describing how the man froze in its headlights and was shot with an arrow while dazed at his computer. Dilbert is seen hiding in a tree, listening to the story. Another moose is impressed that the hunt was done without opposable thumbs.
punchline: The joke reverses the usual hunting story, with moose hunting humans like deer in headlights, and compares the trance-like focus of programmers to a frozen deer, making them easy prey.
summary: Moose swap hunting stories in which people are the prey, and the programmer who stares at his screen is the easy target.

title: Morning Amnesia Spares Dilbert Dread

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ugh... What time is it?... Where am I?... Who am I?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Must be morning... Is this a work day? Do I have a job?... Is it worth getting up for?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Morning amnesia": Nature's way of keeping you from waking up screaming.

setting: Dilbert's bedroom
situation: Dilbert wakes up groggy in bed, confused about the time, his location and even his own identity. As his memory returns he wonders whether it is a work day and whether getting up is worth it. The caption then explains that this brief forgetfulness is nature's way of sparing people from waking up screaming.
punchline: The brief confusion on waking is a mercy, because once you remember your job and your life you would wake up screaming.
summary: A groggy man in bed slowly recalls his life and job, and the narration says forgetting is a blessing that keeps him from screaming.

title: Cult Resume Shows Gullibility

transcript.speaker: Applicant

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Can you chant?

setting: Dogbert's office, with a desk and chair
situation: A man applies to join the Dogbert Cult and hands Dogbert his résumé. Dogbert reads it and notes that the man has already been fleeced by several spiritual leaders. The applicant points out that this proves he lacks independent thought, which makes him an ideal recruit.
punchline: The applicant's history of being swindled by other cult leaders is presented as a qualification, since it shows he is perfectly gullible and unable to think for himself.
summary: A job-style interview for cult membership turns a history of being scammed into the ideal credential for a follower.

title: Maid Promoted to Industrialist Myth

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.text: Dogbert is teaching me capitalism.

transcript.text: Right?

transcript.speaker: Dorgy
transcript.text: Apparently there is flaw in system.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yeah, but we blame it on the Japanese.

setting: Dilbert's home or an open space, with plain backgrounds
situation: Dilbert asks Dorgy why he is dressed as a maid, and Dorgy explains that Dogbert is teaching him capitalism. Dorgy believes hard work as a maid will earn him a promotion to industrialist, but he realizes the system doesn't work that way. Dogbert admits the flaw exists but says they blame the Japanese for it.
punchline: The promise that hard work leads from menial labor to the top is a flawed myth, and the system's defenders simply scapegoat a foreign nation when it fails to deliver.
summary: A naive little dog in a maid costume learns that the supposed ladder of upward mobility is broken, while his mentor cheerfully assigns the blame to a foreign country.

title: Defense Lawyer Presents Hooded Executioner Client

transcript.text: But does this look like a person who could kill??

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ooh! Ooh! I know this one!!

setting: Courtroom during a trial
situation: A defense lawyer addresses the jury and gestures toward his client, who is a shirtless man in a black executioner's hood holding a large axe. The lawyer asks rhetorically whether this looks like someone capable of killing. Dilbert, sitting on the jury, eagerly raises his hand as if answering a quiz question.
punchline: The defendant looks exactly like an executioner, so the lawyer's rhetorical question has an obvious answer, and Dilbert's eager 'I know this one!' treats it as a trivia question.
summary: A lawyer's attempt to prove his axe-wielding, hooded client is harmless backfires when a juror enthusiastically answers the rhetorical question.

title: Stamps Are Valuable Because Collected

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why do people collect stamps?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because they're valuable.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Why are they valuable?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because people collect up all the good ones.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: So, you collect stamps because they're valuable, and they're valuable because you collect them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Right.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sounds pretty fulfilling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To be honest, I just do it for the adrenalin rush.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk where he examines his stamp collection
situation: Dogbert asks Dilbert why people collect stamps, and Dilbert explains that stamps are valuable because people collect the good ones. Dogbert points out the circular logic of collecting valuable things that are only valuable because they are collected. Dilbert agrees, then admits he actually does it for the thrill.
punchline: After a circular justification for stamp collecting is exposed, Dilbert undercuts the whole discussion by claiming a hobby as sedate as stamp collecting gives him an adrenalin rush.
summary: A pair of friends pick apart the circular logic behind stamp values, and the hobbyist confesses to an absurdly mild source of excitement.

title: Dogbert Sings the Greens

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm singing the "greens."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is that like the "blues"?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
