transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oooh... my car needs a tune up and I overslept ten minutes baaabee...

setting: Dilbert's home, living room
situation: Dilbert hears noise and finds Dogbert sitting on a small rug strumming a guitar. Dogbert explains he is singing the "greens," a cheerful cousin of the blues with the same beat. He then performs a song whose lyrics complain about trivial everyday annoyances.
punchline: Blues songs lament serious hardship, while Dogbert's "greens" are sung about petty first-world inconveniences like a car needing a tune-up and oversleeping by ten minutes.
summary: A guitar-strumming dog performs a mock-blues number about minor, trivial troubles to show how much less gloomy it is than the real thing.

title: Dinosaur Dad Tosses the Egg

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur with horns
transcript.text: It's your turn to baby-sit the egg, Bob.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: I used to love it when my dad tossed me in the air.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: This dad stuff is easy.

setting: Prehistoric landscape with two dinosaurs
situation: A horned dinosaur hands the family egg to Bob, a green dinosaur, telling him it's his turn to baby-sit. Bob remembers fondly being tossed in the air by his own dad and decides to toss the egg up. The horned dinosaur watches the airborne egg with a gritted-teeth look of horror while Bob cheerfully thinks parenting is easy.
punchline: Bob's cheerful confidence that parenting is easy is based on tossing a fragile egg into the air, which will obviously end badly.
summary: A dinosaur entrusted with watching the family egg gleefully juggles it in the air, blissfully unaware of the disaster he's courting.

title: Dilbert's Wine Metaphor Gets Corked

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To me, a woman is like a fine bottle of wine.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Each one is familiar, yet distinctive and special.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In the wine of life, some people are destined to be cork-sniffers.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a counter or table
situation: Dilbert earnestly compares women to fine bottles of wine, calling each one familiar yet distinctive and special, while Dogbert sits beside him listening. Dogbert then extends the metaphor to point out that some people are destined to be cork-sniffers.
punchline: Dogbert uses Dilbert's own wine metaphor to mock him as a hopeless romantic who will only ever sniff the cork rather than get the wine, implying he'll never succeed with women.
summary: A man's flowery comparison of women to fine wine is turned against him when his dog suggests he is fated to only smell the cork.

title: Dogbert's Servant Fee: One Banana Split

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't tell the ancient dogs I settled for a banana split.

setting: Dilbert's home, then an ice cream parlor counter
situation: Dilbert gratefully holds Dogbert, thanking him for cloning him just in time. Dogbert invokes an ancient dog tradition that Dilbert must serve him for life. In the final panel Dogbert is sitting at a counter eating a banana split, having accepted that instead.
punchline: Dogbert's grand claim of lifelong servitude under 'ancient dog tradition' is dropped for a cheap dessert, and he asks Dilbert to keep his easy price a secret.
summary: A rescued Dilbert is told he owes eternal servitude to his dog, who then happily accepts a dessert in payment.

title: Lucky Penny Gets Dilbert Soaked

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Look, a lucky penny in the street...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Sploosh

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A penny doesn't go as far as it used to.

setting: A suburban street and sidewalk
situation: Dilbert notices a penny lying in the road and leans over to pick it up. A passing car drives through a puddle and drenches him with a big splash. Soaking wet, he makes a dry remark about the penny while Dogbert looks on.
punchline: Dilbert twists the saying about inflation, pennies being worth less, into a comment on how his lucky penny only got him a soaking, since it clearly didn't bring him luck.
summary: Stooping to grab a coin from the road, a man gets drenched by a speeding car and wryly jokes about the diminished value of a cent.

title: Dilbert Brags About Monogamy, Dogbert Mocks

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm just a one-woman kind of guy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some guys like to play the field. Not me. I'm happy with just one woman.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just one. Uno. That's best for me.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You can take her for rides in the space shuttle you'll never have either.

setting: Dilbert's home, with Dilbert and Dogbert at a low counter or sofa
situation: Dilbert proudly announces to Dogbert that he is a one-woman kind of guy, repeating his preference for a single partner across all three panels. Dogbert finally responds by pointing out that Dilbert has no woman at all, comparing her to a space shuttle he will never have either.
punchline: Dilbert presents his lack of romantic prospects as a principled choice for monogamy, and Dogbert sarcastically exposes that he has no woman, just as he has no space shuttle.
summary: A single, lonely engineer insists he prefers just one woman until his dog deflates the boast by noting he has none.

title: Dogbert Fails Dog License Test

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Impossible!

transcript.speaker: Clerk
transcript.text: For example, this question on "natural enemies": The correct answer is "mailman." You wrote-in "fax machine."

punchline: Dogbert insists the bureaucracy is outdated, since in his modern view a fax machine has replaced the mailman as a dog's natural enemy.
summary: A dog fails his licensing exam by naming a technological gadget instead of the traditional foe, then accuses the bureaucracy of being behind the times.

title: Dilbert Meets Coffee-Drinking Microchip

setting: Inside Dilbert's computer
situation: Dilbert is sucked into his computer, where he meets a small microchip character who invites him to have coffee. Dilbert asks whether chips really drink coffee and whether it makes them irritable with each other. The microchip cheerfully hugs a giant coffee pot and reveals it has killed all the other chips.
punchline: The caffeine-fuelled microchip answers a question about irritability by casually admitting it murdered every other chip, so it no longer has anyone to be irritable with.
summary: A jittery chip inside a computer explains that heavy coffee drinking solved its conflicts with colleagues through mass murder.

Dilbert nervously asks him to leave the flamethrower outside, and the cleaner grumpily says they may as well give in to the mildew.
punchline: The cleaning person looks like a violent punk and brings a flamethrower as his cleaning tool, then sulks that without it the mildew wins.
summary: A man's new housekeeper turns out to be a menacing, flamethrower-wielding punk who treats mildew as an enemy to be incinerated.

punchline: Dilbert concludes that the lessons only cost six dollars because the instruction is so bad that students plummet to the ground and crash.
summary: A bargain-priced skydiving course delivers its student straight onto a coworker's desk, explaining the suspiciously low fee.
keywords: you get what you pay for

situation: Dilbert sits in a chair at a therapy session describing his compulsion to enter hardware stores. His therapist, who has been taking notes, interrupts to complain that Dilbert only talks about himself and never about her feelings. When Dilbert points out he's paying $75 an hour, she scolds him for being selfish.
punchline: The therapist has the roles reversed, demanding that the paying patient listen to her problems and calling him selfish for expecting the therapy he's paying for.
summary: A paying patient is chastised by his own therapist for hogging the session with his problems instead of attending to hers.

title: Lab Rat Suspects Macaroni Experiment

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: (thought) Macaroni and cheese causes paranoia...

setting: A scientific laboratory
situation: A lab rat confronts the scientist who runs the experiment, complaining that he is fed an absurd amount of macaroni and cheese every day. He says he once believed it was hospitality, but now suspects a sinister motive. The scientist, taking notes on a clipboard, quietly thinks that macaroni and cheese causes paranoia.
punchline: The rat's growing suspicion is itself the experimental result, since the scientist is secretly testing whether macaroni and cheese causes paranoia.
summary: A suspicious laboratory rat questions his endless pasta diet, unaware that his doubts are exactly what the researcher is recording.

title: Denture Invention Ate Johnson

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert, asking whether his automatic denture invention mistook a coworker named Johnson for a meat loaf. Dilbert casually admits it happened last April and that he should have mentioned it. The Boss slumps with his face in his hand while Dilbert asks if there is paperwork to complete.
punchline: Dilbert treats a fatal accident caused by his invention, concealed for months, as a mere administrative oversight and asks about the paperwork instead of showing any remorse.
summary: A manager learns an engineer's gadget devoured a colleague months ago, and the engineer's only concern is whether he skipped a form.

setting: Dilbert's home office with a computer desk and a telescope
situation: Dilbert calculates that an asteroid will hit Earth in a couple of minutes, and Dogbert panics, apologizes for his past misdeeds, and vows to give his last minute to the poor. Dogbert then realizes Dilbert isn't panicking and learns the asteroid is only golf-ball sized. It crashes into Dilbert, knocking him and his chair over.
punchline: Dogbert's fake deathbed conversion was pointless because the asteroid was harmless, and the tiny impact still flattens Dilbert, leaving Dogbert to shrug off any deeper meaning.
summary: A dog's panicked change of heart over an incoming space rock proves unnecessary when the object turns out to be tiny, though it still topples his owner.

title: Mother Hugs Loaf Instead of Baby

setting: A park bench outdoors
situation: Dogbert notices a woman on a park bench cradling a loaf of French bread as if it were her newborn. She realizes her baby was mixed up with the bread at the grocery store and worries her son Jimmy may have been put in a toaster. She finds the real baby in the grocery bag, admits she bonded with the bread, and Dogbert jokes about not eating sandwiches at her house.
punchline: After a grocery store mix-up swaps her baby with a loaf of bread, the mother casually admits she bonded with the bread, prompting Dogbert to dryly worry about her habit of treating food like family.
summary: A mother absent-mindedly cradles a baguette, discovers her actual infant in the shopping bag, and confesses her accidental attachment to the pastry.

title: Dilbert and Eve: Nothing to Wear

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ... and women have always played hard to get...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then how about a date next year?

transcript.speaker: Eve
transcript.text: I'd love to, but I don't have a thing to wear.

setting: Dilbert's armchair at home, then the Garden of Eden
situation: In the first panel Dilbert sits in an armchair, lecturing Dogbert that women have always played hard to get. The second panel, captioned 'Dilbert and Eve', shows Dilbert in the Garden of Eden with a snake draped around his neck, asking a naked Eve for a date next year. She declines by saying she has nothing to wear.
punchline: Eve's excuse that she has nothing to wear is a classic brush-off line, but it is literally true because she is in the Garden of Eden, so the rejection is both a joke about dating and about Adam and Eve's nakedness.
summary: A man's theory about hard-to-get women plays out in paradise, where the first woman turns him down with a wardrobe excuse that happens to be literally accurate.

title: Honest Dinosaurs Go Extinct

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's this business of you climbing on the roof and shouting when I'm at work?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Sorry. We dinosaurs have always been bad at concealing our feelings. . . in fact. . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: "Honesty caused the extinction of many early species."

transcript.speaker: Spiny creature
transcript.text: Don't let the spines fool you; I'm great eating!

setting: Dilbert's home, then a prehistoric scene
situation: Dilbert arrives home from work and confronts his pet dinosaur about climbing on the roof and shouting while he is away. The dinosaur apologizes, saying dinosaurs can't hide their feelings. The final panel shows a dinosaur about to eat a small spiny creature that has just honestly told it that it tastes good.
punchline: Being completely honest about your feelings or your own weaknesses is dangerous, which explains why honest species like the dinosaurs died out.
summary: A scolded pet dinosaur admits it can't hide its feelings, and a prehistoric aside shows how brutal candor can be for survival.

title: Dogbert Counsels Clueless Dinosaur Couple

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Just do what comes naturally.

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You're doomed.

setting: Dogbert's consulting session, with two dinosaurs seated on the floor and Dogbert in an armchair
situation: Two dinosaurs, one green and one gray with long antlers, ask Dogbert for advice on how to have an egg. Dogbert tells them to simply do what comes naturally. They reply with an absurd idea about rolling in Jello and yodeling, showing they have no idea how reproduction works.
punchline: The dinosaurs' absurd interpretation of 'what comes naturally' shows they are hopelessly clueless, so Dogbert bluntly declares them doomed, which also hints at their extinction.
summary: Two baffled dinosaurs seek advice on making an egg and reveal such a ridiculous idea of nature that their adviser gives up on them.

punchline: The dinosaurs' hard-won 'survival lies' are the same tired self-flattering fibs humans tell, claiming to avoid tabloids and only watch the news and educational programming.
summary: Two dinosaurs proudly show off the only lies they have learned, which turn out to be the familiar claims people make about avoiding trashy tabloids and watching only worthy television.

summary: A jailed Dogbert uses his single phone call to hire wreckers to flatten the building holding him.

summary: Two would-be defectors are expelled by their cult leader and instantly plead to return, proving to him why their species lost out.

summary: A researcher gets a peer-pressure-prone rodent to down a beer with a single lazy line, then confesses he enjoys tormenting test animals more than anything else about his job.

summary: A flush lottery winner makes a ridiculous bulk order at a burger joint while a passing dog grumbles privately about people like him.

summary: A senior citizen gives feminism the credit for the end of catcalls, and a sardonic dog suggests she is out of touch with reality.

transcript.text: Don't tell anybody-- there might be a stigma.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy hill, then beside a garbage can
situation: Dogbert begs a garbage man to repair Dilbert's cloning device so Dilbert can be brought back to life. The garbage man casually says he has the right parts in his truck and begins tinkering with the device on top of a garbage can. Dogbert realizes the plan involves cloning Dilbert from his own garbage, and the garbage man asks him to keep it quiet.
punchline: The garbage man treats cloning a person from his own trash as a routine job, and his only worry is that people might look down on it.
summary: A sanitation worker nonchalantly fixes a futuristic gadget to resurrect Dilbert from refuse, concerned only about how it will look.

title: Skeptics Flee Chicken Demonstration

transcript.speaker: Moderator
transcript.text: Welcome to another meeting of the "Skeptics Society."

transcript.speaker: Moderator
transcript.text: Tonight we will use scientific methods to debunk Edna Griffin's claim that she can turn an audience into a flock of chickens.

transcript.speaker: Moderator
transcript.text: We'll need some volunteers...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Motion to adjourn...

transcript.speaker: Audience Member
transcript.text: Whoa, look at the time!

setting: A meeting hall where the Skeptics Society is gathering
situation: The moderator of a Skeptics Society meeting announces that the evening's activity is to debunk a woman's claim that she can turn an audience into chickens, and asks for volunteers. The audience, Dilbert included, suddenly panics and rushes to end the meeting and leave.
punchline: The supposedly skeptical audience is secretly afraid the chicken-transformation claim might be true, so they bolt rather than volunteer.
summary: A club of self-proclaimed doubters loses its nerve the moment it is asked to test a magician's claim on themselves.

title: Inspiring Memo Prompts Day Off

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "Urgent memo to all employees:"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh. Looks important.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "If we are to remain competitive, you must proactively improve quality on all actionable items!"

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow! That was inspiring. My heart is pounding. I'm all tingly...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd better take the rest of the day off...

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits in his cubicle and reads an urgent memo to all employees. The memo is full of empty management jargon about proactively improving quality on actionable items. Dilbert reacts as if he had a physical reaction, then decides he needs to go home.
punchline: The memo is so vacuous and unmotivating that Dilbert sarcastically claims it was inspiring, using his supposed racing heart as an excuse to leave work early.
summary: A buzzword-filled company memo leaves one engineer so "inspired" that he declares he needs the afternoon off.

title: Yanking a Loose Thread, Losing Head

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Loose thread.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't remember if it's better to cut these or just yank on them.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Thoop!

setting: Plain purple background, no specific location (Dilbert alone)
situation: Dilbert notices a loose thread on his shirt and thinks aloud about whether to cut it or pull it. In the second panel he turns away and grabs the thread. In the final panel he yanks it and his head pops off his body.
punchline: Dilbert pulls the loose thread without cutting it, and the result is that his head comes clean off, so yanking was clearly the wrong choice.
summary: A man tugs at a stray thread on his shirt and learns the hard way that some things shouldn't be pulled.

title: Dinosaur Coworker Mocks Dilbert's Tools

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Looks like another shopping binge at the hardware store.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't resist.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gee, Bob, what did dinosaurs do before tools were invented?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: It was hard...

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Sometime, you should try to tighten a Phillips screw with a fern.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's no way to live.

setting: Office or cubicle area
situation: Bob the dinosaur comments on Dilbert's bag of purchases from the hardware store, and Dilbert admits he couldn't resist buying more tools. Dilbert then asks, while holding a wrench, how dinosaurs managed before tools existed. Bob replies that it was hard and describes trying to tighten a screw with a fern.
punchline: The dinosaur's dry answer reveals that life without tools meant absurd struggles, like using a plant to turn a Phillips screw, and Dilbert can only agree it's no way to live.
summary: A gadget-loving engineer quizzes his prehistoric coworker about life before tools and gets a deadpan description of fern-based screwdriving.

title: Dogbert's Miracle Hose Water Scam

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Goodbye... I think your "New Age Mineral Water Spa" has been a complete rip-off!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm sorry you feel that way... Here's a free gallon of miracle hose water.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're an evil little dog.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Thirsty?

setting: Outside the entrance of Dogbert's New Age spa
situation: A dissatisfied customer storms out of Dogbert's so-called New Age mineral water spa, calling it a rip-off. Dogbert responds by blasting her with a hose and calling it free 'miracle hose water'. Dilbert, watching, calls him evil, and Dogbert coolly offers him a drink.
punchline: Dogbert reveals his 'mineral water' is just ordinary hose water, and meets a justified complaint by mocking the customer and cheerfully threatening to do the same to Dilbert.
summary: A scammer dog answers a refund-seeking customer by drenching her with a garden hose and pitching the spray as a freebie.

title: Dogbert's Three Stages of Grief

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The three stages of grief

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Denial

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No... Dilbert can't be dead.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Anger

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll kill the scum who did it!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Economics

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: No expensive caskets. Just wrap him in newspapers; he would have wanted it that way.

setting: Dogbert's home, on a rug and then at a desk
situation: Dogbert goes through the stages of grief over Dilbert's death, labeled in captions. He starts in denial, moves to anger and vows revenge, then skips straight to economics. In the last stage he decides to save money on the funeral by wrapping Dilbert in newspapers instead of buying a casket.
punchline: The final 'stage' of grief is not acceptance but cheapness, as Dogbert coldly cuts funeral costs and claims Dilbert would have wanted it that way.
summary: A grieving dog runs through denial and rage before settling on the real concern: how to bury his friend as cheaply as possible.

title: Dilbert Sucked Into Computer, Meets Michael Chip

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh! I'm being sucked into my own computer program!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've always feared this...

transcript.speaker: Michael Chip
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Michael -- Michael Chip.

transcript.speaker: Michael Chip
transcript.text: Cover charge is two bits. ...Get it?

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle, then inside his computer program
situation: Dilbert, sitting at his desk, realizes he is being pulled headfirst into his own computer program, something he has always feared. He ends up inside the digital world, where a small caped character introduces himself as Michael Chip and demands a cover charge of two bits.
punchline: The computer-world greeter is named Michael Chip and charges 'two bits' as a cover charge, a pun on the old slang for twenty-five cents and the computing unit of data.
summary: A programmer gets pulled bodily into his own software and is greeted by a pun-loving mascot who asks for a data-themed entrance fee.

title: Baby Dinosaur Inherits Both Parents' Traits

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: Our baby!!

transcript.speaker: Gray Dinosaur
transcript.text: He's got my looks!

transcript.speaker: Baby Dinosaur
transcript.text: Hey, where am I? I'm all confused.

transcript.speaker: Green Dinosaur
transcript.text: He's got your brain, too!

setting: A rocky prehistoric landscape with a nest on a rock ledge
situation: Two dinosaur parents watch their egg hatch. The gray parent proudly says the baby has inherited his looks. The newly hatched baby then announces he is confused, and the green parent points out that he inherited the gray parent's brain as well.
punchline: The green parent's remark that the baby also got his mate's brain is an insult, implying the gray dinosaur is dim-witted and has passed that on to the child.
summary: Proud parents admire their newborn until the baby's befuddled first words reveal an unflattering inherited trait.

title: Waiter's Threatening Tip Guide

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: I've taken the liberty of calculating a twenty-percent tip.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: It's written on the back next to a picture of a smiling diner... A fifteen percent tip is shown by the picture of a guilty-looking diner.

transcript.speaker: Waiter
transcript.text: Below that is a picture of a diner and his dog with salad forks in their backs...

setting: A restaurant table
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert are finishing a meal when the waiter presents a tip calculation card. He explains that a twenty-percent tip earns a smiling diner picture and fifteen percent earns a guilty-looking one. Below that, a picture shows a diner and his dog with salad forks in their backs, an implied threat for tipping too little.
punchline: The waiter's tip guide escalates from friendly suggestion to a violent threat against stingy customers and their pets.
summary: A waiter hands over a cheerful tipping chart that ends with a menacing illustration of what happens to diners who underpay.

title: Project Hype Means Project Doom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your new project will be vital to the performance of this company!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The more he talks it up the stupider the project must be.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: ...high visibility, a chance to excel and be noticed!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In fact, I stand to salute you for the job you will be doing! You're what makes this country great!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does this have anything to do with the janitors' strike?

setting: The Boss's office
situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert a new project, praising it as vital, highly visible and a chance to be noticed. Dilbert privately concludes the project must be terrible because of the over-the-top hype. When the Boss starts saluting him and talking about what makes the country great, Dilbert guesses the real reason: he is being asked to fill in for the striking janitors.
punchline: The Boss's inflated praise for the 'vital' project was a cover for assigning Dilbert janitorial work during a strike.
summary: A manager lavishes grand praise on an assignment, and the engineer correctly suspects it is a menial job nobody wants.

title: Impatient Investor Calls His Broker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ahem... I think I'll call my stock broker... I'm an investor, you know.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ooh... I'm impressed.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What? No profits yet? I'll call back in an hour.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wonder if this is a bad time to be in chocolate coins.

setting: Dilbert's home, at a desk with a telephone
situation: Dilbert shows off to Dogbert that he is an investor and phones his stock broker. He is shocked to learn he has made no profits yet and says he'll call back in an hour. Afterward he worries aloud that he may have invested at a bad time in chocolate coins.
punchline: Dilbert expects instant profits from his investment, and the fact that he put his money in chocolate coins shows how naive and poorly chosen his investing is.
summary: A boastful new investor demands quick returns from his broker, then frets that his odd choice of holdings may have been ill-timed.

title: Dilbert's Blind Date Banned Buffet

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert greets his blind date

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: This is the biggest woman I've ever seen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... hi.

transcript.speaker: Blind Date
transcript.text: Hi

transcript.speaker: Dilbert (thought)
transcript.text: I have only one chance of financially surviving dinner.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Say... why don't we go to the "all-you-can-eat house of starch and pasta"?

transcript.speaker: Blind Date
transcript.text: Can't... banned for life.

setting: Doorway of Dilbert's home at the start of a blind date
situation: Dilbert opens the door to greet his blind date and is startled by how large she is. Worried about the cost of feeding her, he suggests an all-you-can-eat pasta restaurant as his only affordable option. She replies that she has been banned from it for life.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to dodge an expensive dinner fails because his date has already eaten so much at the all-you-can-eat place that she was permanently banned.
summary: A nervous man hopes a cheap buffet will save his wallet on a blind date, only to learn his enormous-appetited date has been kicked out of it forever.

title: Dogbert's Moral Dilemma With Ray Gun

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: On one hand, I know it's wrong to use Dilbert's invention to blow up these empty mail trucks.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: On the other paw, this is gonna be more fun than sneezing on strangers.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a moral dilemma... but I like to think that difficult choices like this build character.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Click

setting: An empty lot beside a chain-link fence with parked mail trucks in the background
situation: Dogbert stands outdoors holding a ray-gun-like device that Dilbert invented, planning to blow up empty mail trucks. He briefly weighs the ethics, decides the fun outweighs the guilt, and then fires the weapon.
punchline: Dogbert dresses up his gleeful destructiveness as a character-building moral struggle, but he never seriously considers not doing it.
summary: A dog debates the ethics of vaporizing parked postal vehicles with a borrowed gadget, then pulls the trigger anyway while congratulating himself on his integrity.

title: Dogbert Plots Static Electricity Revenge

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I can feel the static electricity building . . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Shuffle shuffle shuffle shuffle

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Shuffle shuffle

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Shuffle shuffle

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I most certainly will not call you "Thor, Dog of Thunder."

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Prepare to die.

setting: Dilbert's home, in front of a bulletin board
situation: Dogbert shuffles his feet across the floor to build up static electricity, his fur puffing out more with each panel. He intends to zap Dilbert. Dilbert, towering over the fluffed-up dog, flatly refuses to give him the grandiose name he wants.
punchline: Dogbert's grand plan to become the fearsome "Thor, Dog of Thunder" is undercut by the fact that he is just a small, static-puffed dog threatening his owner with a shock.
summary: A small dog fluffs up with static from shuffling his feet, planning a shocking revenge on the man who won't give him a mighty new name.

title: Dogbert Writes Senator About Opera

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dear Senator, I demand a constitutional amendment barring the obscene and anti-American lyrics in opera.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What makes you think a Senator will care about an issue like that?

transcript.speaker: Senator
transcript.text: I think we found another issue to keep us from working on real problems.

transcript.speaker: Aide
transcript.text: Ooh-ooh!

setting: Dogbert's office, then a senator's office
situation: Dogbert writes a letter to a senator demanding a constitutional amendment against obscene and anti-American opera lyrics. Dilbert doubts a senator would care about such an issue. In the final panel, a senator reading the letter cheerfully says it gives them another way to avoid real problems while an excited aide cheers.
punchline: Politicians welcome trivial, symbolic issues because they provide an excuse to avoid tackling the difficult problems they should be solving.
summary: A ridiculous letter about opera lyrics is gleefully welcomed by a legislator as a handy distraction from actual governing.

title: Dilbert's Frog Curse Palace Infiltration

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: By now Dilbert should have infiltrated Buckingham Palace.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: One kiss from the Princess and his "frog curse" will be lifted...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I just hope his disguise works...

transcript.speaker: Voice from a window
transcript.text: Charlie, why does your breath smell like flies?

transcript.speaker: Charlie
transcript.text: Uh... I had lunch with a common person today...

setting: A bare room with a wall clock, then the exterior of a brick tower
situation: Dogbert stands alone thinking that Dilbert, who he says is under a frog curse, should have sneaked into Buckingham Palace by now to get kissed by the Princess, and he hopes the disguise works. In the final panel, someone at a tower window asks a visitor named Charlie why his breath smells like flies. Charlie, evidently Dilbert in disguise, covers by saying he lunched with a commoner.
punchline: Dilbert's disguise is a thin cover story, since his breath smells like flies because he is a frog, and he explains it away as the result of dining with a common person.
summary: A scheming dog sends his frog-cursed friend to a royal palace hoping a princess's kiss will break the spell, but the disguised amphibian's fly-scented breath nearly gives him away.

title: Computer's Subliminal Messages Revealed

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: A microchip gives Dilbert the tour inside his computer.

transcript.speaker: Microchip
transcript.text: ...So you see, it's mostly a trick...

transcript.speaker: Microchip
transcript.text: We've been sending you subliminal hypnotic suggestions through the video display for years.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Like what?

transcript.speaker: Microchip
transcript.text: Goofy stuff, like "Computers are fun" and "Put all of your pens in your shirt pocket."

setting: Inside Dilbert's computer, then a blank backdrop
situation: A microchip creature gives Dilbert a tour of the inside of his computer. It confesses that the machine has been sending subliminal hypnotic suggestions through the screen for years. The suggestions turn out to be things like believing computers are fun and keeping pens in a shirt pocket.
punchline: Dilbert's nerdy habits, like loving computers and carrying pens in his shirt pocket, are revealed to be the result of his computer's mind control.
summary: A tiny guide inside a PC admits the machine has secretly programmed its owner's most stereotypical geeky habits.

title: Stolen ID, Stolen Job

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I got fired.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The crook who robbed our house used my company I.D. card to steal my job too.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All I have is you, my friend.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Don't you hate it when they say continued

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert tells Dogbert he has been fired, explaining that the burglar who robbed their house used his company ID card to take his job as well. In the last panel a dejected Dilbert sits in a corner and tells Dogbert he is all he has left, and Dogbert answers with a puzzled 'Dogbert?'. A caption notes the story continues in the next strip.
punchline: Having lost his possessions and his job to the same thief, Dilbert clings to Dogbert as his only friend, and the strip ends on a deadpan cliffhanger, with the 'continued' caption mocked as a letdown.
summary: A burglar who ransacked the house also impersonated Dilbert at work, leaving him jobless and desperate for the companionship of his dog.

title: Dogbert Denies Dilbert's Hair Loss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I'm losing my hair.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't be silly. You aren't losing your hair.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not? Oh, good.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: How could you possibly lose these huge clumps...

setting: Dilbert's bathroom
situation: Dilbert looks into a hand mirror in the bathroom and worries aloud that he is losing his hair. Dogbert reassures him that he is not, and Dilbert is relieved. Then Dogbert is shown holding clumps of Dilbert's hair, implying he has been plucking it out.
punchline: Dogbert's reassurance is a lie, as he is the one who has been pulling out Dilbert's hair in huge clumps, and he admits it only after Dilbert is comforted.
summary: A balding man is soothed by his dog's denial until the dog's hairy evidence gives the game away.

title: The Engineer's Snorting Curse

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: Working hard?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hardly working! Giggle giggle snort!!

transcript.speaker: Bald coworker
transcript.text: You snorted.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was my best line of the day... then I snorted.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The curse of the engineer.

setting: Office cubicle and a hallway, early Dilbert era
situation: A bald coworker in glasses stops by Dilbert's cubicle and asks if he is working hard. Dilbert answers with a joke, 'Hardly working', and then giggles and snorts at his own wit. Afterward Dilbert laments that the snort ruined his best line, and Dogbert diagnoses it as the curse of the engineer.
punchline: Engineers are so socially awkward that even when they finally deliver a good joke, their own snorting laughter ruins it.
summary: A witty quip loses all its charm when its nerdy delivery ends in an embarrassing snort.

title: Dogbert Zaps Dilbert Over Puns

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe since you're full of static electricity, you should say "It is useless to be a resistor." Hee-hee-hee.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: ZAP!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nothing annoys the "Dog of Thunder" quite as much as nerd puns.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert makes a nerdy pun to Dogbert, who looks fluffy and static-charged. Dogbert responds by delivering an electric shock that turns Dilbert into a glowing X-ray skeleton. Dilbert is left scorched and smoking while Dogbert explains that nerd puns annoy him.
punchline: Dogbert, in his "Dog of Thunder" persona, retaliates against a bad nerd pun by literally electrocuting the person who made it.
summary: A clumsy electrical wordplay earns Dilbert a painful jolt from his unamused pet.

title: Dogbert Coaxes Dilbert's Head Out

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: After tugging a loose thread on his shirt...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do something.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hmm... Head got sucked into torso, huh?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll try flattery... Your head will expand and pop right out...

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Later

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: ...and you are superior to mollusks in every way but looks....

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I felt something that time.

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: After pulling a loose thread on his shirt, Dilbert's head gets sucked into his torso, and he asks Dogbert to do something. Dogbert decides to try flattery, reasoning that Dilbert's head will swell with pride and pop back out. After a while Dogbert's compliments turn into backhanded insults, and Dilbert says he felt something that time.
punchline: Dogbert's flattery degrades into a backhanded insult (superior to mollusks in every way but looks), and that is the line that finally gets a reaction from Dilbert.
summary: A cartoon engineer whose head has vanished into his shirt is treated by his dog with compliments that gradually sour into insults.

title: Dogbert Seeks Diplomatic Immunity Scam

transcript.speaker: Ambassador
transcript.text: Why have you come to the embassy of the nutty radical country of Pingo-Pongo?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want a job as a diplomat.

transcript.speaker: Ambassador
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm trying to get in on the "diplomatic immunity" scam.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I want to drive cars over people's lawns... I want to fire automatic weapons in any direction!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Ha ha ha ha ha!! I want to throw Jello at politicians!

transcript.speaker: Ambassador
transcript.text: How do we know we could trust you?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sir! I am insulted by your question!

setting: Office of the embassy of the fictional country Pingo-Pongo
situation: Dogbert applies for a diplomat job at the embassy of a nutty radical country, an ambassador in a crown and polka-dot robe interviewing him. Dogbert openly admits he wants diplomatic immunity so he can cause mayhem like driving over lawns and firing weapons. When the ambassador asks if he can be trusted, Dogbert acts offended.
punchline: Dogbert candidly confesses he only wants the job to exploit diplomatic immunity for reckless behavior, then feigns outrage when his trustworthiness is questioned.
summary: A scheming dog tries to become a diplomat solely to get away with outrageous misdeeds, then takes offense at being doubted.

title: Dilbert's Ego Seeks a Toupee

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I know you; you're Dilbert's ego.

transcript.speaker: Ego
transcript.text: Correct.

transcript.speaker: Ego
transcript.text: I disowned him. He just wasn't feeding me enough.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What can a little ego do to feed itself?

transcript.speaker: Ego
transcript.text: Which way to the toupee store?

setting: A plain room with a green wall and blue floor
situation: Dogbert meets a small, hairy, walking creature that turns out to be Dilbert's ego. The ego says it left Dilbert because he wasn't feeding it enough. Dogbert wonders how an ego can feed itself, and the ego asks for directions to the toupee store.
punchline: The ego looks like a toupee itself, so its idea of feeding its vanity is to go and buy more hair, which is a vain, superficial fix.
summary: A neglected ego that has walked out on its owner sets off to satisfy its vanity at a hairpiece shop.

title: Dilbert's Ego Wears Toupee, Brags

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Nice toupee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Ego
transcript.text: Thanks.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Ego
transcript.text: It's the "Roy Orbison" model. I am now ready to hit the dating scene.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Really? You drive a Porsche?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's Ego
transcript.text: It's red... but enough about me.

setting: A teal-walled room, then a bar
situation: Dogbert compliments a small, fleshy creature labeled as Dilbert's ego on its Roy Orbison-style toupee and sunglasses. The ego announces it is ready to start dating, then is shown at a bar chatting up a woman with a martini. It boasts about its red Porsche before pretending to change the subject.
punchline: The ego brags about owning a flashy red Porsche, then hypocritically says 'enough about me' to feign modesty while having just shown off.
summary: A personified ego in a cheesy wig and shades heads to a bar and slyly flaunts a sports car to impress a woman.

title: Dogbert Insults Butcher's Cured Ham

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Do you have cured ham?

transcript.speaker: Butcher
transcript.text: Right here.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boy, if that's cured, what does a sick one look like?!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've always felt a duty to share my gift of mirth with others.

setting: A butcher shop's meat counter, then the street outside
situation: Dogbert asks a butcher behind a deli counter whether he has cured ham, and the butcher points to the display case. Dogbert wisecracks that if that is cured, a sick ham must look terrible. Walking away down the street, Dogbert says he feels obliged to spread his sense of humor around.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses his own mean-spirited, groan-worthy pun as a generous 'gift of mirth,' when it was really just an insult to the butcher's product.
summary: A talking dog mocks a butcher's meat with a pun and then pompously frames his rudeness as a public service.

title: Dogbert Directs Dilbert Versus Godzilla

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A home video?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Dogbert versus Godzilla." We'll use Bob the Dinosaur as Godzilla and you can be Raymond Burr!

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Shouldn't Godzilla get top billing?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Quiet on the set!!

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: Dogbert is letting me be the "key grip."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Darn! All I got was the Raymond Burr role.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: In this first scene, Bob, you rip the arms off the "Ken" doll while Barbie and Skipper watch in horror.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dilbert, you'll be eating a cheeseburger and the shock waves will cause you to smoosh it into your face.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Then I come in and waste both of you with a fire extinguisher.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Raymond Burr dies?

transcript.speaker: Dinosaur
transcript.text: What, no sequel?

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dogbert arrives with a camera and megaphone to direct a home video, 'Dogbert versus Godzilla', casting Bob the Dinosaur as Godzilla and Dilbert as Raymond Burr. He directs a silly, destructive plot involving toy dolls and a cheeseburger, then reveals that he will kill both actors with a fire extinguisher.
punchline: Dogbert, as director, gives himself the heroic role and casually has the cast killed off, leaving the actors to complain about trivial matters like billing and sequels.
summary: A bossy dog filming a monster-movie parody at home assigns the parts, outlines an absurd script, and ends it by dispatching his own cast.

title: Dogbert's Atlantis Past-Life Scam

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Welcome to Dogbert's New Age Mineral Water Spa... hand over the cash.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Hold it... the vibes from my crystal tell me we knew each other in a previous life... in Atlantis!

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: That's what you told the last guy, too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Atlantis was a small town. I ran the only donut shop.

setting: Reception desk of Dogbert's New Age mineral water spa
situation: Dogbert runs a New Age spa and demands cash from a customer waiting in line. Mid-transaction he claims his crystal reveals they knew each other in a past life in Atlantis. The customer points out he has used this line on others, and Dogbert shrugs it off with a made-up story about running the only donut shop in Atlantis.
punchline: Dogbert is caught using a fake past-life connection as a sales trick, and instead of denying it he doubles down with an absurd excuse that explains why he'd know everyone.
summary: A scheming dog running a mystical spa tries to charm a paying customer with a fabricated shared history and then brushes off the accusation with a ridiculous alibi.

title: Dogbert Meets Soviet Exchange Dog

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert meets the Soviet-exchange program dog.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: He seems harmless.

transcript.speaker: Soviet Dog
transcript.text: Greetings, Comrade Dogbert.

transcript.speaker: Soviet Dog
transcript.text: I have come to learn capitalist system from dog's perspective.

transcript.speaker: Soviet Dog
transcript.text: ...And your god is this Donald Trump?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't think it's official yet.

setting: Outdoors, with Dogbert in a toy tank and a visiting dog in a fur hat
situation: Dogbert, sitting in a tank, thinks the visiting Soviet exchange dog looks harmless as it greets him. The visitor explains he has come to study capitalism from a dog's perspective. Later, as they sit on rugs, the visitor asks whether the capitalist god is Donald Trump.
punchline: Dogbert's reply that it isn't official yet implies that worship of wealthy tycoons like Trump is practically the established religion of capitalism.
summary: A visiting Soviet dog hoping to understand capitalism wonders if Donald Trump is its deity, and Dogbert dryly says the title hasn't been made official.

title: Aerosol Spray Meets Ozone Hole

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: For years Mother Nature had been dropping hints about the ozone problem.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Aaah... Pine-cone fresh lemon scent.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Fssst

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Flash!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The direct approach would work no better.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it unseasonably warm today?

setting: Outdoors on a sunny day, with an opening panel showing Earth from space
situation: A narrator explains that nature has long been hinting at the ozone problem, while Dilbert happily uses an aerosol air freshener. A blinding flash from above shows his skeleton, and he is left scorched, smoking and nearly stripped of clothes. Dogbert watches from the corner as Dilbert, oblivious, wonders whether the weather is unseasonably warm.
punchline: Even when the ozone layer visibly fries him for using aerosol spray, Dilbert fails to connect the cause and effect, only noting that it feels unusually warm.
summary: A man sprays his scented can, gets zapped by the sun through the damaged atmosphere, and still doesn't grasp what's going on.

title: Dilbert's Christmas Wish for Understanding

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What do you want for Christmas, Dogbert?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The usual: domination of Earth, happiness at the expense of others, personal ego gratification.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And you?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I want to feel greater love and understanding for other people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Even obnoxious and cynical people?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And people who laugh at you for being an idealistic simpleton?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yeah.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Merry Christmas, Dilbert.

setting: Dilbert's home, sitting in front of a fireplace with Christmas stockings
situation: Dilbert and Dogbert sit by the fireplace at Christmas while Dilbert asks what Dogbert wants as a gift. Dogbert lists selfish, world-dominating wishes, then asks about Dilbert's wish and probes whether his hoped-for love would extend even to cynics and those who mock him. Dilbert sincerely says yes, and Dogbert warmly wishes him a merry Christmas.
punchline: Cynical Dogbert, after testing Dilbert's idealism with pointed questions, shows a rare moment of affection and respect for his owner's sincere good nature.
summary: Beside the fireplace, a scheming dog and his earnest owner swap holiday wishes, and the dog's mockery softens into an unexpectedly tender greeting.

title: Secretary Dreams of Acting or Medicine

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As your new supervisor, I want to discuss your career path.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're a secretary now, but what do you want to be in two years?

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: A famous actor... or maybe a doctor.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh... I don't think I can help you here...

transcript.speaker: Secretary
transcript.text: Oh, right, but you'll expect me to work hard for you.

setting: Office, at the secretary's desk
situation: Dilbert, newly promoted to supervisor, holds a career-path discussion with his secretary. She says she wants to become a famous actor or a doctor in two years. Dilbert admits he can't help with that, and she points out that he'll still expect her to work hard for him.
punchline: The supervisor's career-path talk is meaningless because the secretary's ambitions have nothing to do with the job, yet she is still expected to keep working hard for him.
summary: A new boss asks his secretary about her future goals, only to learn her dreams lie far outside the company while her duties stay the same.

title: Accounting Department's Reality-Creating Numbers

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert is forced to work in the accounting department

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: First you must understand how numbers change reality...

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Some people think numbers merely reflect reality... but we believe that numbers create reality.

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: This is our budget-erasing room...

transcript.speaker: Accountant
transcript.text: Erase faster!!

setting: A cave-like accounting department populated by green, troll-like creatures
situation: Dilbert is sent to work in the accounting department, where a pointy-hatted troll-like accountant lectures him with a sign reading 'Numbers change reality.' The accountant claims numbers create reality, then shows him the budget-erasing room, where goblin-like workers frantically erase figures while being whipped to go faster.
punchline: The accountants treat budget figures as magic that can reshape reality, and their 'budget-erasing room' reveals the numbers are simply being manipulated and erased by overworked drudges.
summary: A monstrous accountant gives Dilbert an orientation on how finance supposedly bends reality, culminating in a dungeon of creatures erasing budgets under the lash.

title: Dilbert's Boring Surgery Story Puts Dogbert to Sleep

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Dogbert! I'm home after my second major surgery in two weeks!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...So after the first operation they discover that a tiny convict and a nurse had hidden inside my torso to escape...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Boy...it sure is hard to keep a medical story interesting.

setting: Dilbert's home living room
situation: Dilbert arrives home and announces he has just had his second major surgery in two weeks. Sitting in an armchair, he launches into an absurd tale about a tiny convict and a nurse hiding inside his torso. By the last panel he realizes Dogbert has fallen asleep and remarks on how hard it is to keep a medical story interesting.
punchline: Dilbert has to make up a ridiculous tale to hold a listener's attention because even surgery stories bore people, and Dogbert falls asleep anyway.
summary: Fresh from yet another operation, a man spins a wild fictional tale of stowaways inside his body, only to find his dog dozing off.

title: Senator Bans Opera Without Risk

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Senator Newt Axxes' office

transcript.speaker: Senator Axxes
transcript.text: Mister Dogbert makes a strong argument for banning opera.

transcript.speaker: Aide
transcript.text: The polls show that almost nobody cares about this issue... There's virtually no political risk in embracing it!

transcript.speaker: Senator Axxes
transcript.text: So I can keep getting elected?

transcript.speaker: Aide
transcript.text: Until they scrape your festering corpse out of that chair!

setting: Senator Newt Axxes' office
situation: A senator sits at his desk holding a paper and says that Dogbert has made a good case for banning opera. His aide explains that polls show nobody cares about the issue, so supporting the ban carries no political risk. The senator asks whether this means he can keep getting elected, and the aide cheerfully replies with a gruesome remark about his corpse.
punchline: The aide's sarcastic reply implies the senator is so entrenched in office that voters will keep re-electing him until he literally dies in his chair.
summary: A politician happily adopts a position because polls say nobody will object, and his aide darkly notes he'll stay in power until death.

title: Obscene Opera Lyrics Are Foreign

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm writing to protest the obscene lyrics in opera.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's not obscene... it's a foreign language.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh... I thought I was just living a very sheltered life.

setting: Dilbert's desk at home or in the office
situation: Dogbert sits at a desk writing a letter of protest about obscene lyrics in opera. Dilbert points out that the lyrics aren't obscene, they're just in a foreign language. Dogbert responds that he thought he was merely sheltered.
punchline: Dogbert mistook unintelligible foreign lyrics for obscenity, and his deadpan reply suggests he assumed anything he couldn't understand must be dirty, or that his sheltered life kept him from knowing such words.
summary: A complaint letter about dirty opera lyrics collapses when it turns out the words were simply in another language.

title: Dilbert Asks Mechanic About Oil

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just a quick question: is it necessary to change my oil...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...or can I just keep letting it run dry and then add new oil?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think the answer is going to be "no" to that second option.

transcript.speaker: Mechanic
transcript.text: Aaaeeeoo

setting: An auto service shop
situation: Dilbert asks a mechanic whether he really needs to change his oil or can just keep adding new oil whenever the engine runs dry. The mechanic is so horrified by the idea that he drops his cap and rag and then falls over backward screaming. Dilbert calmly concludes that the answer to his second option is no.
punchline: The mechanic's extreme, screaming collapse is the answer to Dilbert's absurd question, which Dilbert deadpans as a clear "no."
summary: A man's ridiculous plan to skip oil changes so appalls a garage mechanic that the mechanic keels over in horror.

title: Dilbert's Sunday Paper Ruined

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh good, Dogbert isn't around.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can read the Sunday paper without having to share.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ahhh... Mine are the first hands to unfold its crisp little pages. I alone will determine the order of reading.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Nobody will blurt out the punchlines before I read them.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Were you finished with this section?

setting: Dilbert's living room
situation: Dilbert gleefully settles into his armchair to read the Sunday paper, delighted that Dogbert isn't around to share it or spoil the comics. Dogbert then drops in from above and sends the chair flipping over with Dilbert's legs sticking up, newspaper scattered everywhere. Dogbert calmly asks if Dilbert is finished with the section.
punchline: Dilbert's smug plans to enjoy the paper in peace are wrecked when Dogbert violently upends him, then politely asks for the section as if nothing happened.
summary: A man relishes having the Sunday paper all to himself until his dog crashes in and casually asks for a turn.

title: Misreading Date's Body Language, Chainsaw

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can tell what my date is thinking by her body language.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Her body is telling me "Let's cuddle by a fireplace..."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: "I'll get some firewood," she says...

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Vrooooom

setting: A restaurant table on a dinner date
situation: Dilbert sits at a dinner table, confidently claiming he can read his date's thoughts from her body language. He imagines she wants to cuddle by a fireplace, and that she is offering to fetch firewood. In reality she stands over him revving a chainsaw, which suggests a very different intention.
punchline: Dilbert's confident reading of his date's body language is hopelessly wrong, since her real intent seems to be to attack him with a chainsaw rather than cuddle.
summary: A hopeful man interprets his date's gestures as romantic, never noticing she has pulled out a roaring chainsaw.

title: Hitchcock's Sequel: The Fish

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Let's go see the new Alfred Hitchcock movie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How could there be a "new" Hitchcock movie?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's some kind of a sequel.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alfred Hitchcock presents The Fish

setting: Dilbert's living room, then a movie theater
situation: Dogbert suggests going to see the new Alfred Hitchcock movie, and Dilbert objects that Hitchcock is long dead so there can't be a new film. Dogbert says it's a sequel. The final panel shows the movie screen, where a Hitchcock-like figure reads a newspaper while goldfish swim around him, titled 'The Fish'.
punchline: The 'sequel' is a spoof of Hitchcock's thriller 'The Birds', with the birds replaced by harmless goldfish, and Dogbert's logic of a sequel doesn't explain how a dead director made it.
summary: A dog proposes seeing a fresh film from a long-dead director, and the screen reveals a silly fish-themed follow-up to a famous bird-attack thriller.

title: Dogbert Joins Anti-Fur Movement

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I've decided to join the anti-fur movement.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that hypocritical? You wear a fur coat every day.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Oh...yeah, never mind...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Wait...

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert sits at his computer while Dogbert announces he is joining the anti-fur movement. Dilbert points out that Dogbert wears a fur coat every day, so Dogbert abandons the idea. In the last panel Dogbert stands alone, thinking 'Wait...'.
punchline: Dogbert drops his principled stand the instant he is reminded of his own hypocrisy, then belatedly realizes the fur coat is just his own body.
summary: A dog hastily joins a cause, backs out when challenged, and only afterward realizes that the fur coat in question is simply his own.

title: Dogbert Admits Flushing Dilbert's Sweaters

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) The great thing about dogs is their loyalty.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I flushed all of your sweaters down the john, because it was fun.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: (thought) Dogs are honest, too.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I'll do it again Ha ha ha!

setting: Dilbert's living room at home
situation: Dilbert sits in an armchair thinking fondly about how loyal dogs are. Dogbert, perched on the arm of the chair, calmly confesses that he flushed all of Dilbert's sweaters down the toilet just for fun. Dilbert then reflects that dogs are honest too, and Dogbert cheerfully promises to do it again.
punchline: Dilbert's idealized view of dogs as loyal and honest is shattered by Dogbert, who is honest only about his own mischievous disloyalty, and who gleefully vows to repeat it.
summary: While his owner daydreams about canine devotion, a smug dog cheerfully owns up to destroying his wardrobe and promises more of the same.

title: Dogbert's Absurd Unauthorized Dilbert Biography

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you really going through with the unauthorized biography of me?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'm up to the part where Jackie "O" and Liz Taylor fight a duel for your love.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Tragically, neither are aware that you're carrying Steve Garvey's baby!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Tap tap tap

setting: Dilbert's office or home, at a desk with a computer
situation: Dilbert asks Dogbert whether he is really writing an unauthorized biography of him. Dogbert, typing at the computer, cheerfully describes the fabricated plot: two famous women duelling over Dilbert. He then adds that neither knows Dilbert is carrying a celebrity athlete's baby, and keeps typing.
punchline: Dogbert's 'biography' is wildly fictional and increasingly outlandish, showing that an unauthorized biography owes nothing to the truth.
summary: A dog cheerfully types an invented, tabloid-style life story of his owner full of celebrity duels and scandalous pregnancy claims.

title: Dilbert Protests Tissue With Sandpaper

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Every single tissue box has a feminine design.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Men have noses too. This is sexist. I can't support this practice.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sandpaper?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I had to make a statement.

setting: A grocery store aisle, then a home kitchen counter
situation: Dilbert is shopping and notices that every tissue box has a flowery, feminine design. He decides it is sexist and refuses to buy them. At home, Dogbert finds that Dilbert has bought sandpaper instead, which Dilbert says was his way of making a statement.
punchline: Dilbert's principled protest against feminine tissue boxes leaves him blowing his nose on harsh sandpaper, so the only person he really punishes is himself.
summary: A man too offended by flowery packaging to buy soft tissues ends up with abrasive sandpaper as his protest.

title: Frog Dilbert Fooling Lady Di

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert needs a kiss from a princess to remove the frog curse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's hopeless...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's one chance, but we'll need some props.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You seriously think this will fool Lady Di?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'd wait until she's had a few margaritas.

setting: A home interior, with Dogbert rummaging in a closet
situation: Dilbert has been turned into a frog and can only be cured by a princess's kiss. Dogbert fetches props from a closet and dresses the frog with a crown and a large fake nose, hoping to pass him off as a prince to Lady Di. Dilbert doubts the disguise will work, and Dogbert says to wait until she's drunk.
punchline: The disguise is so unconvincing that the only way it could fool the princess is if she were drunk on margaritas.
summary: A cursed frog gets a flimsy disguise from his dog, who admits it will only pass if the princess is tipsy.

title: Dinosaur Babysitter Meets Yuppie Bigots

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Hi. I'm Bob. I called earlier about the baby-sitting job.

transcript.speaker: Homeowner
transcript.text: To be honest, we didn't know you were a dinosaur when you called...

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: That's okay. I didn't know you were yuppie bigots.

setting: Front doorway of a suburban house
situation: Bob, a green dinosaur, arrives at a house to interview for a babysitting job he arranged by phone. The man at the door admits they didn't realize he was a dinosaur when he called, hinting at rejecting him. Bob calmly replies that he didn't know they were bigots either.
punchline: Bob turns the homeowner's prejudiced hesitation around by labeling the couple as yuppie bigots, exposing their discrimination.
summary: A dinosaur arriving for a babysitting gig gets a cold reception and answers the homeowner's prejudice with a calm insult of his own.

title: Getting Rich: Inheritance and Crime

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: You see, Dorgy, under our capitalist system anybody can become rich.

transcript.speaker: Dorgy
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Inheritance and crime are the most popular methods.

transcript.speaker: Dorgy
transcript.text: Which is preferred method?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's best to have your parents do the crime and let you inherit it.

setting: Dogbert's rug-covered meeting area, with Dorgy wearing a tall green hat
situation: Dogbert lectures Dorgy, a hat-wearing dog sitting beside him on a rug, about how anyone can get rich under capitalism. When Dorgy asks how, Dogbert says inheritance and crime are the most popular routes. Dorgy asks which is preferred and Dogbert recommends combining them.
punchline: Dogbert cynically suggests the best way to get rich in a supposedly open capitalist system is to inherit the proceeds of your parents' crimes, implying wealth comes from privilege and wrongdoing rather than merit.
summary: A cynical dog tutors his apprentice on how wealth really gets made, and the answer is family crime passed down as an inheritance.

title: Runaway Lab Rat Lacks Willpower

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: Ahaa! There's my runaway lab rat! I'd recognize little XP-39C² anywhere!

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: All is forgiven. Come back to your job at the lab. I love you.

transcript.speaker: Scientist
transcript.text: He was specially bred to have no will power.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Hold me.

setting: A pink-walled room, apparently Dilbert's workplace, with a scientist visiting
situation: A lab scientist in a white coat spots Ratbert and claims him as his escaped lab rat, XP-39C². He declares everything forgiven and begs the rat to return to his job at the lab. While Dilbert looks on, the scientist explains the rat was bred to have no will power, and Ratbert immediately asks to be held.
punchline: The rat's supposedly engineered lack of will power is confirmed instantly when he caves to the scientist's affection and asks to be held, so the escape was never really under his control.
summary: A researcher reclaims his escaped test animal with affection, and the creature's engineered spinelessness makes it surrender on the spot.

title: Dilbert's Honesty Backfires on Date

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: What I look for first in a man is honesty.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... I'd like to skip this boring conversation and go smooch.

transcript.speaker: Date
transcript.text: I didn't mean honesty about relevant things.

setting: A restaurant table on a date
situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman who says honesty is the first quality she looks for in a man. Dilbert takes her at her word and bluntly says he finds the conversation boring and would rather skip ahead to kissing. She reacts with shock and clarifies that she did not mean that kind of honesty.
punchline: Dilbert takes the woman's call for honesty literally and tactlessly insults her conversation, and she retreats to saying she only wanted honesty about relevant things, which exposes that people want selective honesty.
summary: A woman praises honesty on a date, then recoils when her companion candidly admits he finds talking tedious and wants to kiss instead.

title: Dogbert's Wrecking Company Escape Plan

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Don't worry, Killer, I'll get us out of this pound by nightfall.

transcript.speaker: Killer
transcript.text: How?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I used my one phone call to call a wrecking company to destroy this place.

transcript.speaker: Killer
transcript.text: That sounds dangerous to me.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Coming up: a near-death experience or possibly just a stupid dream sequence.

setting: A dog pound cell
situation: Dogbert and a poodle named Killer are locked in a dog pound. Dogbert promises to free them by nightfall and reveals he spent his one phone call hiring a wrecking company to demolish the building. The final panel is a teaser caption over a rubble-strewn scene with the poodle lying injured among the wreckage.
punchline: Dogbert's escape plan is to have the pound demolished with them still inside, and the strip openly mocks its own sitcom-style teaser by promising a near-death experience or a stupid dream sequence.
summary: A scheming dog's solution to getting out of the pound is to hire a demolition crew, and the strip ends by gleefully teasing the resulting wreckage.

title: Dogbert Wants Playing God Advertised

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert and Dilbert are called for jury duty.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: What a stupid waste of my valuable time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's your civic duty. It's the small dues you pay for living in a just and free society.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Big whoopee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you get to play God with other people's lives.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Well, they should say that in the letter.

setting: Dilbert's home or office, with a summons letter in hand
situation: Dogbert and Dilbert have both received jury duty summonses. Dogbert complains that it wastes his valuable time, and Dilbert lectures him about civic duty and the dues of living in a free society. When Dilbert mentions that jurors get to play God with other people's lives, Dogbert says that perk should have been in the summons.
punchline: Dogbert is only interested in jury duty once he learns it gives him power over other people's lives, and he complains that the summons should have advertised that selling point.
summary: A reluctant dog grumbles about being summoned to court until his friend mentions the godlike power jurors hold, which he finds far more persuasive than civic virtue.

title: Teaching Sex Ed From TV Guides

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Okay, class... put your weapons away and open your TV Guides.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Timmy, please read aloud the passage from "Falcon Crest" under the Friday listings.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: There's got to be a better way to teach sex education.

setting: A classroom, with Dogbert standing on a teacher's desk
situation: Dogbert plays a teacher addressing a class of armed students. He has them open TV Guides and asks Timmy to read the soap opera listing for Falcon Crest aloud. In the last panel he thinks to himself that sex education must be possible to teach some better way.
punchline: Dogbert's sex education curriculum consists of reading racy TV soap listings, and even he privately admits it is a poor method, while the students bringing weapons to class hints at how rough the school is.
summary: A teacher-dog runs a rowdy classroom lesson built on television listings and quietly doubts his own approach to teaching sex ed.

title: Doctor's Half-Off Life Expectancy Sale

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Normally I'd give you six months to live.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: But we're having a "50% off sale" today, so I'll give you a full year for the same price.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: And you get an extra ten days if you pay cash!

setting: Doctor's examination room
situation: Dilbert sits on an exam table in a paper gown while a doctor delivers a terminal prognosis. The doctor then treats the remaining lifespan like a retail product, offering a half-off sale and a bonus for paying cash. By the last panel Dilbert has slumped over the table in despair.
punchline: The doctor markets life expectancy like a store promotion, applying sales gimmicks and cash discounts to a death sentence, which mocks commercialized healthcare.
summary: A physician pitches a grim diagnosis as a clearance deal, tossing in bonus days for anyone paying in cash.

title: Dogbert Gets the Knitted Elbow Warmer

transcript.speaker: Aunt Helen (note)
transcript.text: Dear Dilbert, I hope you like this elbow warmer I knitted for you. Love, Aunt Helen

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's an elbow warmer; just a thoughtful little gift from me to you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I feel like the lowest creature in the gift chain.

setting: Dilbert's home
situation: Dilbert reads a note from his Aunt Helen that came with a hand-knitted elbow warmer. He then passes the gift along to Dogbert, presenting it as a thoughtful present from himself. Dogbert, wearing it on his snout, realizes he is the end of the regifting line.
punchline: Dogbert points out that being handed down an unwanted gift makes him the bottom of the food chain, a pun on the 'gift chain' of regifting.
summary: A useless knitted present from a relative gets passed down to the dog, who sourly notes his place at the bottom of the regifting hierarchy.

title: Computer Predicts Women Always Cry

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I programmed my computer to analyze any situation and predict the female response.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This should clarify a few things.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll type in "watch sad movie."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Result: Crying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I'll try "receive flowers."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Result: Crying.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Let's try "date with Dilbert."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Result: Crying.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Boy, the truth gets vicious when you corner it.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle
situation: Dilbert has programmed his computer to predict how women will respond to situations and tests it with inputs. Watching a sad movie and receiving flowers both return crying, which seems plausible. When he enters a date with himself, the result is also crying, and Dogbert comments on the harsh result.
punchline: The computer's prediction that a date with Dilbert makes a woman cry reveals the uncomfortable truth that his dating prospects are dismal, and Dogbert wryly notes the truth turns vicious when cornered.
summary: A nerdy engineer's homemade prediction program gives the same tearful answer to every scenario, including the one he was secretly hoping would turn out better.
